Mr. Speaker, I think this is an unfortunate bill. It is regrettable that we have at this time to be dealing with the bill in the House. I totally reject what the previous speaker said with respect to this bill.
I think the government had an opportunity over the past two years to negotiate with the hospital employees and with the ships' crews to reach a conclusion to this collective agreement that would be fair for all concerned, would be fair for people throughout the country and would avoid even the perception of an emergency taking place now-something which many people reject-which would motivate this bill and force us to deal with it at this time.
The real problem is that over the last two years the government has been motivated by its own ideological inability to deal in good faith with its employees. I share the opinion of another speaker in this House who spoke on this legislation yesterday who indicated that nowhere is the government's ideological problem in terms of dealing with trade unions more evident than in its relations with its employees in the postal system. That single corporation has five times as many grievances against it as compared to any corporation of a similar size operating in Canada. The type of labour relations that take place at the Post Office is provocative and destructive of employee-management relations. That type of destructive and provocative labour relations is characteristic of this government and characteristic of its agencies.
What we are dealing with here is not a problem of negotiating between an employer and an employee, the problem is that the employer is ideologically motivated and ideologically hampered, being the reason that we
December 8, 1989

have difficulty with the negotiations between the Government of Canada and its employees.
I was not surprised to see in the explanations contained in the last annual report of the post office that a tremendous amount of money-millions of dollars-had been spent by the Post Office in hiring scabs, for preparing and training them to break the strike at the Post Office and to provoke the employees of the Post Office. That action precipitated a great deal of violence on the picket line and many people were seriously injured. This left a residuum of bitterness that will govern employee relations between the Government of Canada and the postal workers for a long time to come. One cannot argue that that same type of bitterness has not overflowed into other wage disputes that this government has had with its employees. This particular strike is no example.
I do not have one of the components in my riding that will be affected by this dispute, the hospital employees' component, but I certainly do have the ships' crew component which is front and centre and very evident in my riding. We have Coast Guard establishments up and down the west coast of Vancouver Island. We have lifeboat crews at Bamfield and Tofino which put out to sea every day in rough conditions to protect the lives of mariners and to protect vessels and their cargoes, as well as the people who use the west coast of Vancouver Island in what has been traditionally called the graveyard of the Pacific. These men and women in the Coast Guard risk their lives virtually every day in the service of Canadians and in the service of the maritime industries that serve Canada. '
We also have the ships' crews aboard naval tugs, Coast Guard vessels, research vessels and other Coast Guard ships that service buoys and light stations and other Department of Transport facilities up and down the coast. Yet in spite of the critical work that these ships' crews do up and down the coast of British Columbia and throughout my riding, this government does not seem to have attached as much importance to them as it should have over the last two years when it should have been bargaining in good faith with those employees with a view to reaching a settlement with them. As I said before, it appears that the ideological problems that this government has with trade unions is probably the main
Government Orders
barrier that prevented it from reaching an agreement with those employees.
When I look at what ships' crews earn in the federal service on the west coast of Canada it is clear to me that the employees have a very solid case for improvement in their wages and working conditions. For example, a seaman in the federal service makes $11.68 on the west coast, while B.C. ferry employees in the same position make $16.49 an hour and those in a similar position with the Stena Line, a privately-owned line operating on the west coast, make $15.53 an hour. Thus private-sector crews make 33 per cent more than those in the federal service. Those in the provincial public sector working for the B.C. Ferry Authority make 41 per cent more than the crews working in the federal Public Service-and that is after the results of this settlement have been included in the wage rates.
So there is no question that the employees of the federal government working for the Coast Guard, on research vessels, on naval tugs and other fisheries ships in the federal Public Service definitely have a case for improving their wage rates and for bringing them in line with the wages being earned by other people doing similar jobs but under less dangerous conditions on the west coast. The ships' crews for the federal service are not even asking for parity. They are asking simply for a reasonable wage rate.
Look at the fact that the average wage of the hospital employees is $18,000 and the average wage of the ships' crews is $23,000, and the fact that many of these employees are sole supporters of their families in many parts of the country. Even though they are working hard, even though they are risking their lives, and even though they are dedicated to the Public Service of this country, they are still living at or below the poverty line, depending on what region of the country they live in. That situation should be redressed. The government should have seen the necessity to redress that situation and should have negotiated in good faith and with commitment to those employees to the point that a collective agreement could have been reached long before now and that those situations which are totally unacceptable should have been redressed long before now.
We are very proud of the workers in the Coast Guard on the west coast in my riding. They do terrific work on behalf of the people of Canada. Even during this strike, working on a voluntary basis, Coast Guard workers have taken lifeboats out and have rescued people on the west coast of Canada. They have made it a policy during this strike that they will defend the life, health and safety of persons, but not necessarily of property. They have gone out in stormy and difficult conditions. They have

rescued people on a volunteer basis at personal or union expense during the period of this strike. They have said that they will never let the people of Canada down. They will provide those emergency services. They will be available to the people of Canada when they are needed during the strike even though they are on strike.
It is the government that has let the people of this country down and that has delayed a collective agreement for so long. The reason for this-and I cannot repeat this too often-is an ideological problem that the government has of negotiating in good faith with its employees. Why else would these crews be paid so much less than their counterparts in the public service in the provinces and those in the private sector? Why would they be paid so much less than those people when their jobs are so much more critical and so much more important because of the involvement of risk to life, health and safety?
It is the government that is at fault for this problem. I suspect that the government has delayed this issue so long because it knows that in the end it has the power to come into the House of Commons to hold legislation of this type like an axe over the heads of the workers. It knows that it can undermine the process of collective bargaining by having this axe.
It is interesting to note that the minister responsible for the Treasury Board is the minister not only negotiating with the employees but the one who has brought this legislation into the House of Commons. On the one hand he knows that he has the axe that he can use to cut off negotiations, forcing those people back to work under whatever conditions he chooses because he has the majority in the House. On the other hand he seems to believe that he is capable of negotiating in good faith. That just is not happening.
After long protracted negotiations during this strike there were people in my constituency who actually suffered physically as a result of violence on the picketline. An employer recommended that employees who are not part of this bargaining unit-and in fact who are not even citizens of Canada but Americans working on testing American weapons at a Canadian naval facility-use their cars or trucks to bump their way through the
picketline. As a result a picketer in my constituency was injured and hospitalized with broken vertebrae as a result of violence on this picketline, violence said to be recommended by an employer. Even today charges have not been laid against that American citizen who committed the act.
Serious problems have resulted as a consequence of the frustration experienced by the employees who were trying to negotiate with the government in good faith, but who saw no good faith coming from the other side of the negotiating table.
There is a serious problem here, a problem of regional equity, a problem of gender equity and other problems that have to be dealt with. In this country in this day and age these problems should not really be part of negotiations. It should be taken without it being said that people who do the same work, whether on the west coast of Canada, the Arctic coast of Canada or on the east coast of Canada should be paid at precisely the same rate, given that their jobs are precisely the same and fall within the same classifications. A lot of the things we are discussing should have been dealt with years ago in the collective agreements of these people.
It is interesting that the only time the national government recognizes that there might be an emergency is when the St. Lawrence freezes up. When the St. Lawrence freezes up and no matter happens on the St. Lawrence River seems to become a national emergency. Then we legislate everybody back to work on both coasts because this government seems to view a very small part of Canada as the most important part and the rest seems to be forgotten in its deliberations. That is a serious problem which is certainly evident in this case. Conservative after Conservative has stood up and indicated that the problem of the imminent freezing of the St. Lawrence Seaway system and the lakes is the problem and the reason we have to legislate these people back to work.
You know what the weather conditions are in this country. You know when the freeze-up comes. You should have felt compelled to negotiate and to achieve a settlement in anticipation of that change in weather this winter. Instead you sat on your duffs. You knew at the very end of it that you could rely on coming into this

House to force those workers back to work using the scanty argument you are using at this point.
I feel that there is a need for a type of bargaining between the federal government and its employees that takes the political impediments of the government in power away from the bargaining system. Let us look at the facts and whether or not in this particular instance the workers have been unreasonable. We are talking about men and women who have not been treated fairly and who are not being treated fairly even now. I believe that this particular legislation shows the government's inability to understand the fundamentals of pay equity, that is equal pay for work of equal value.
I suspect that all members will know that the human rights commission ruled that the hospital services group is under-valued and under-paid. It is true that the classification system was changed but only equalization payments were made, proper adjustments were not made.
With respect to the ships' crews group, we are talking about wages, hours of work, sea duty allowance. In the case of the hospital services groups, we are talking about elderly patients who are now dependent upon volunteers for feeding, cleaning and all normal services. There have been many such indications, and I shall not repeat them. There is $6 million worth of summer navigational aids in the Great Lakes seaway system alone that are at risk because they are out in the freezing waters. There are at least two. One is a question of fairness and the other one is a question of trust. How can one trust and how can one feel that one is being treated fairly when you realize that you are among the lowest paid groups? In some particular groups, the majority are women. How can you feel comfortable with government when you know that you are being paid badly and when you are, in fact, part of a group that has been discriminated against over many years?
It is quite clear that people generally no longer trust the government and that is no news to members opposite. If they look at some of the most recent newspaper reports and the polls that they will see that this is true. They do not believe that this government has been fair, is being fair, or can be fair. If you look at the record, you can see why this is so.
This is the government that propelled us into a trade deal with the United States when, at one time, their leader had said that there would be no free trade with
the United States. He even ridiculed members of his party who were forthright enough to say that they thought it was a wise move on their part. This is the same government whose leader indicated that Air Canada was not for sale. What's happened? It has now gone.
This is the same government whose leader, or at least one minister and probably more, indicated that there would be no unemployment insurance changes. Of course, we know what has happened there.
This is the government that really attempted to persuade Canadians that rather than destroying the rail system, it would invest in the system. You will recall some of the statements made by prominent members of government before they came into power that they would invest rather than destroy. What has happened now? Half the system has been closed down. Over 2,700 people will suffer. Some of those people have been calling constituency offices throughout the country. What a Christmas present for the 2,700 plus people, and their spouses and children.
This is the government that said it would maintain the transfer payments to the provinces for health and education. What has happened? In 1986, they were reduced by 2 per cent and in the last budget by another 1 per cent. There will be $24 billion less given to provinces for health and education over eight or nine fiscal years because of the decisions made after the government said that it would maintain that formula.
Why the malaise? Let us talk about some of those 31 tax increases during the last five years. We are talking about a goods and services tax which is to be imposed and well over 80 per cent of Canadians are saying it is vicious, unnecessary and insensitive. This is a government that has doubled the debt in five years. Yet, it likes to tell us that it is being fair with Canadians, that it knows how to manage the country and the economy. This is the government that failed in 1985 to reduce benefits to seniors. It came back with the clawback and, of course, have been able to get the seniors finally. How can anyone trust this government? It tries one way and fails, then comes back and gets you another way. This is a government that imposed cutbacks to organizations who

are advocates for women and advocates for native groups.
Part of the platform of this government was that its leader was a great conciliator and negotiator. There is tension everywhere in this country. It is time to go back to the negotiating table. It is a time to negotiate in

Mr. Speaker, I rise somewhat reluctantly in support of this bill because I believe that it is a most unfortunate and regrettable circumstance that makes necessary the legislation that exists in Bill C-49.
I believe that one of the most fundamental rights in a democratic society is the right to free collective bargaining. Indeed, on behalf of the individual, one of the most fundamental rights is the right to withdraw one's labour, providing all contractual agreements have been met, if one is unsatisfied with the circumstances in which one finds oneself and, indeed, in accordance with the free collective bargaining process. Of course, that is what this legislation does. This legislation necessitates the disruption of the free collective bargaining process.
However, I must point out at the same time the reason why I am prepared to support this legislation is because the government of the day, the Government of Canada, has a responsibility to see to the interests and the needs of all Canadians, and has a responsibility to see to the safety of Canadians where that safety is imperilled.
It is one of those unfortunate circumstances which happen from time to time, where principles come in conflict, one with the other, and the responsibility of government is not to be effusive with its rhetoric so much as to respond to its responsibilities by doing that which the national need compels.
Indeed, the same responsibility exists, to some extent, for the leadership of collective bargaining associations, the leadership of unions. It is obviously their responsibility to seek the best terms possible for their members. It is also their responsibility to see to the interests of their
members by achieving contracts that will give them the best possible deal under the circumstances and to take that deal back to the members and indicate, in a fair and honest way, that that is the best that can be achieved under the circumstances, and not to needlessly put people in a position where they are either forced into or seemingly forced into going on strike or find themselves remaining on strike beyond the point that makes sense or beyond the point that is in their interest.
I know it is a very contentious issue that brought about this strike situation. I note that in my own province of Nova Scotia, there is a very strong divergence of opinion on the issues among those who are members of the bargaining unit and who voted-and I noted that it was only a very narrow vote-in the locals to which I refer by which the decision was taken.
In the final analysis, the government must see to its responsibility. It must see to the public interest, and in this case the public interest involves public safety. Canadians must be able to count on the Coast Guard to rescue them when their lives are in peril at sea. Canadians at sea and those aboard the vessels of other nations must know that the navigation aids that are there to prevent tragedies and accidents at sea are, in fact, the ones that are supposed to be there.
With respect to the other part of this strike, Canadian veterans must be able to count on being given proper care in hospitals. Canadians have a right to expect this and want them to have it.
Others can speak of the St. Lawrence Seaway, hospitals in Quebec, or the situation on the west coast. Quite frankly, my main concern is that a week ago Monday the lobster season opened in southern Nova Scotia. Twenty-five hundred lobster fishermen are going to sea every day. I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, it is not a very pleasant experience to go to sea in December. It is very cold, the sea can be high, the winds are high. So far the catches have not been too bad and we are very encouraged by that. The prices are not as high as we would like. The days at sea are very, very difficult. This year winter came early to Nova Scotia, just as it would seem to have come early to Ottawa. It is very hazardous to go to sea in inhospitable circumstances.
On the other hand, people must make a living. Lobster fishermen must take advantage of the limited opportuni-
December 8, 1989

ties that exist for them to pursue their activities. In southern Nova Scotia, our season opens on the last Monday in November and closes at the end of May. However, it is only a very limited period that the lobster harvest is at its best, and it is during those first two or three weeks in the season that every individual is anxious to get out and attend his pots and hope that this harvest will provide the base for the year to come to support the family.
Unfortunately, those hazards mean that lives are in peril every single day. Without the availability of the Coast Guard to answer the call, the risk is even greater. I know that the members of the Coast Guard who provide those near-shore coastal services, with those small vessels out of places like Port La Tour and Clarke's Harbour are particularly concerned because what they are faced with is in conflict with what they know they should be doing. Either way, on either side of this issue, they are good solid members of their organization. They wish to stand with their colleagues in their organization. Indeed they wish reasonable salaries and working conditions. I personally feel that those people are very much underpaid. I would like to see the government continue to increase those salaries and bring them up to levels where they should be so that people do not find themselves in the situation where they have to go on strike.
What we are dealing with, in terms of those people in the Coast Guard, are people who are at the lower end of the scale, notwithstanding the fact that they face very hazardous jobs in very hazardous circumstances on a daily basis. At the same time, those people do not feel comfortable staying at home while friends and neighbours are at sea and their lives may well be imperilled. Many of these men are themselves former fishermen. They know what it is like to be out at sea at difficult times of the year and they want to go back to work.
It might surprise members opposite to know that as a member of Parliament from an area that is very directly affected by this, I have had phone calls from members of the bargaining units who are in fact out on strike saying: "Please can't you get the government to legislate us back to work so that we can have an end to this situation and we will not be forced to come to grips with this unpleasant conflict situation in which we find ourselves".
Government Orders
What are the issues at stake here? Fundamentally, it seems to me, there are two issues which have been the source of controversy in this labour dispute. One has to do with equal rates of pay on the east and west coasts. I must say that as maritimers, and particularly as Nova Scotians, for many years it has grated on us knowing that people on the west coast are paid higher rates of pay for doing precisely the same jobs which our people are doing and indeed often not under as hazardous climatic circumstances.
Nevertheless, I think it is important to note that the breakthrough came in breaking down this villainous principle that had been with us for a long time. I have heard members opposite speak of this. It surprises me that the previous member who spoke, the member from St. Boniface, made reference to it. He seems to have forgotten that this principle of unequal rates of pay was one that became a standard practice through the auspices of the former Liberal government, a government which presumably he would have supported.
I think it is important for this House to recognize that the breaking down of this villainous principle occurred during the past two or three years by the actions of this government. I want to remind all members that it was the former member of Parliament for Halifax, who is no longer in this place, who fought on behalf of the members of that bargaining unit in Halifax and got a break in that principle. We have seen a gradual change begin in the last contract with a one-third amelioration of that principle that started to break the ice, as it were, for what is now on the table. That in fact is an offer that eradicates once and for all this principle.
I do not know why members opposite still get up and speak of this differential because in fact, as per the offer that is on the table right now, this government has finally caught up to the fact that work should be at the same pay on one side of this country as the other. I commend the minister for bringing it here as I commend the former minister and member for Halifax for making it happen in the first place.
The other issue, of course, is whether there is a fair offer on the table. There is no question that the Coast Guard workers, particularly those along the shore, deserve and should have higher salaries and higher wage rates than they have. But the government has a variety of responsibilities. It has a responsibility to all its employees. It has a responsibility to see that where there

December 8, 1989
Government Orders
are people being paid salaries below what they should be, that it raises them as quickly as it can, but the salaries must be fair to all people within the public service.
Therefore I think it is important to note that the offer that has been rejected at this point is an average 5.23 per cent offer, whereas other members of the public service have only received an average rate of 4.2 per cent.
Fifty cents an hour. It can be ended for 50 cents an hour.

I might say, as a Member of Parliament, that I would be quite happy to receive a 5.23 per cent increase. However, percentages are not the beginning and the end of these things, because if the rate is low the percentage naturally should be higher.
It is important for the government to gradually move in the direction of bringing these salaries up. As for the circumstances now, it is important to recognize that the offer that is available at this time is a higher percentage offer than has been received by other members of the public service. Under this bill those people will not only receive that equality, not only receive those increases but, at the same time, will have an opportunity before arbitration to make their case. If it is a just one, quite possibly they will get an even better settlement.
Therefore, I think the bottom line is that the offer which the government has made is fair. The legislation, while regrettable in the sense that it does interfere with free collective bargaining is in the public interest and therefore the government is acting responsibly and properly to introduce this legislation. It will provide an opportunity for this dangerous situation to come to an end, for the people to get back to work. I know they want to get back to work and indeed for this House to get on with the important business of the nation.
Therefore, I would urge all members to support this bill at this stage and subsequent readings.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured to take part in this important debate on the Government Services Resumption Act.
The use of back to work legislation at this time raises some very important questions about the government's role as an employer and as a proponent of pay equity.
I would like to register my deep concerns that the government is imposing the back to work legislation on the employees of the hospital service group and ship crew workers. Historically back to work legislation has been used 20 times over the past 40 years: 10 times to end strikes in the ports and shipping sectors, 5 times to keep the railway operating, twice to get grain handlers back to work, twice to resume postal services, and once to provide for the continuation of air traffic control services.
The majority of these actions were taken when disputes involved strikes, negotiation deadlocks and a definite and immediate danger to the well-being of the Canadian public.
Is there such a national emergency facing us today? The answer to that question is no. We have the workers themselves to thank for that. We should commend these workers for their dedication and commitment in light of the circumstances. The ships workers, for example, have responded to each and every emergency call that has occurred in the past four weeks.
The hospital workers, on the other hand, have also offered to leave the picket lines should an emergency situation arise in National Defence hospitals or veterans homes.
These people are not holding the safety or health of Canadians for ransom. They are simply using the only means available to them to arrive at fair and decent contract settlements.
When there is no immediate danger to the Canadian public, it is difficult to understand the justification for resorting to back to work legislation in the situation we are facing today. Taking away a basic right of Canadian workers cannot be taken lightly and cannot be done lightly. The truth is that the right to strike exists in this country for a reason.
Back to work legislation does not only limit the bargaining power of the striking employees. It seriously limits the government's ability to negotiate an agreement in the best interests of the country. This can be construed as an abdication of the responsibility of both the employees involved and the Canadian public at large.
The use of back to work legislation is generally regarded as negative. When everyone knows that the government has this tool in hand the incentive to reach an agreement through bargaining is weakened. Are
December 8, 1989

there not better ways to foster co-operation and avoid confrontation? In my view there are.
The government has introduced back to work legislation. There is no national crisis at stake. This is an admission that our system of collective bargaining has failed.
Can the government assure Canadians that every effort has been made to arrive at a fair and equitable agreement? Have all the avenues been explored? Is the government willing to go back to the bargaining table? So far the answer is no to all of these questions.
This dispute involves the government on the one side and over 3,500 of the lowest paid members of the Public Service on the other.

The government is employing 2,200 ships' crew employees on Coast Guard vessels, fishing boats, lifeboats and other boats of the Department of Public Works, both on the eastern coast and the west coast and the Great Lakes. Those skilled workers are risking their lives on a daily basis to ensure the safety of margation of sea and on our seaways. Their average salary, which is 16 to 28 per cent less than that of their counterparts in the private sector, is only $21,000.
In the area of hospital services, the government employs 1,200 workers who on a regular basis extend care to our veterans and people in National Defence hospitals and homes. There are nursing attendants janitors, kitchen attendants, and so forth. They are to every patient some kind of an extended family. The majority are women, Mr. Speaker and forty-eight per cent of these workers earn $20,000 a year or less.
They are not striking without reasons. They are on strike because they could not get decent, fair salaries. The issue of equal pay for equal work is central to these two labour disputes.

The Canadian Human Rights Act has three sections referring to the equal pay for work of equal value principle. Equal pay for work of equal value became law for federal public servants in March 1977. The govem-
Govemment Orders
ment has made commitments to Canadians over and over again that work will be judged on its value, on the basis of skill and knowledge, mental and physical effort, responsibility, and the nature of working conditions.
People must not be paid based on which part of the country they live in, whether or not they are man or women, black or white. It is a principle we have endorsed as a government and as a nation. This is what we are all about. This is what Canada is all about.
Fairness is a principle which is extremely important to the productivity and efficiency of our Public Service. Yet here we are in 1989, almost 1990, and coast guard crews working aboard vessels on the east coast are paid $2,000 less than similar crews working on the west coast of our country. They are doing the same job for the same employer and getting substantially less money for it.
At National Defence hospitals here in our city and elsewhere in Canada hospital service workers, the majority of whom are women, have had to fight for over a decade to achieve wage parity with their general service counterparts. They went to the Human Rights Commission because their rates of pay trailed by 10 per cent or 40 per cent the wages of those in the general service category. The Human Rights Commission agreed with them. They were awarded $28 million, the largest pay equity settlement in the history of the Public Service. More than two years later these employees are still not getting the pay they deserve.
Retroactive pay from 1980 to 1987 based on new classifications has not yet been received by these workers. Retroactive pay from 1987 to the present also has not been paid out by the Treasury Board. These hospital workers are living on wages close to the poverty line. On average, they are entitled to an additional $3,000 per year. Given that the salary range of these workers is between $16,000 to $22,000 a year, an additional $3,000 is a lot of money.
The President of the Treasury Board assures us that he is working to comply with the equalization order given by the Human Rights Commission. He has stated that the various stages of the pay equity process are to blame for these delays which are proving so costly.

December 8, 1989
Government Orders
Blaming the delays on the pay equity system is not a valid argument. If we have a system where workers earning poverty level wages must wait for two, three or ten years to get fair wages and pay equity, then I say there is something wrong with that system. We cannot ask these employees to bear this burden.
Our Public Service is already burdened with serious problems such as downsizing and job insecurity, the increasing age of the workforce and the lack of promotion opportunities. Women are still under-represented in upper levels of the Public Service, representing only 12.3 per cent at the management level and 83 per cent in support positions.
So far attempts at employment equity have not been very successful. The matter before us today is only a symptom of the problems facing public servants and their employer, the government. The bottom line is that these workers want a fair deal. As a government, we should be setting an example for the private sector, an example which includes real efforts to address critical issues such as wage equity and constructive collective bargaining practices.
The federal government must be a role model for other employers in this country. It is disheartening to see Public Service employees having to fight for fair treatment from the federal service. The government has told this House that these employees are essential employees and should therefore not be allowed to strike. I would reply that every single public servant in this country is an essential employee. Each one deserves to receive a fair wage for his or her work. Each one, regardless of gender or region, deserves to be paid the same wage as another employee doing a comparable job.
Back to work legislation is not the answer. The striking employees are responsible and dedicated to their jobs. They want to go back to work. The Public Service Alliance has offered to go back to the bargaining table.
This morning we have received a call from Mr. Whalen of the hospital services union who indicated that the President of the Treasury Board's statement that employees were seeking 14 per cent for each of the next three years is an unfair statement. In fact, they are seeking 6 per cent for each of the next three years. He
also said that the dispute is about two issues: resolving the pay equity first and getting the pay increases second.
It is time for the government to make the concerns of these hard working Canadians a priority and resume negotiations. Legislating these workers back will not resolve the deep-seated concerns at issue today. We must work out a fair and equitable solution at the bargaining table, not on the floor of the House of Commons.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today in support of the bill before us, Bill C-49, an act to provide for the resumption of certain government services. As Your Honour can well imagine I will be speaking mainly on the part of the government services provided by federal ship crews.
Late last week, on the advice of the Canadian Coast Guard the Laurentian Pilotage Authority and the Corporation of Lower St. Lawrence Pilots, the Minister of Transport announced that navigation would be temporarily halted on the lower St. Lawrence because safety could not be assured.
Subsequently, on September 4 after a further review and assessment of the situation, it was decided to permit navigation in the lower St. Lawrence with certain restrictions such as daylight navigation and the requirement to have two pilots on board the vessel.
The cold weather has caused earlier than normal ice formations in the river from Tadoussac west. Floating aids have become iced up. Ice floes have moved many others out of position and these now pose a navigational hazard. Still others submerged by the ice will come to the surface as a ship passes by with the risk that the buoy's anchor cable will foul up the ship's propellers. These are among the reasons navigation was temporarily closed between Quebec City and Les Escoumins.
By this time of year Canadian Coast Guard buoy tenders usually have recovered the summer buoys and replaced them with winter aids, but they have been tied up by the strike since November 14. The Seaway's reopening in 1990 could be affected by the loss and displacement of the buoys.
The temporary closure of one section of the waterway left some 100 merchant ships waiting to start or to continue their voyage. In addition, other ships are
December 8, 1989

currently in the seaway system above Montreal and will have to exit the seaway by December 19, the announced clearance date of the shipping season.
Ice-breakers need to be deployed without delay to ensure the safe and orderly exit of these vessels and to assure the safety of ships carrying general cargo and petroleum products to St. Lawrence and seaway ports. These ice-breakers are normally assigned to the Quebec City-Trois Rivieres area from mid-December to midMarch each year. The federal government must step in now to restore safe navigation in the St. Lawrence-Great Lakes and ensure the safety of mariners and fishermen in all parts of Canada.
The St. Lawrence Seaway system is the world's foremost inland waterway, used for decades by ships of every seagoing nation. The provision of essential services such as aids to navigation and ice-breaking are fundamental to the safety and integrity of this ocean link to central Canada and the industrial heartland of the United States.
The provision of these services is a key mandate of the Canadian Coast Guard. We have a long-standing commitment to ensure the safety and efficiency of this route for trading nations of the world. Transport Canada has a reputation of efficient and reliable safety services to shipping and the fisheries. The recent cold weather serves to remind us of the importance of these services, especially search and rescue operations.
Many fishermen who go to sea in the perilous winter months are alive today thanks to the Coast Guard search and rescue efforts. Since the strike began, basic search and rescue services have been provided by Canadian Coast Guard SAR operations through co-operative efforts with the union. I want to compliment the unions on the co-operation that they have shown throughout this labour dispute.
While the arrangement has also allowed for the provision of search and rescue services in life threatening circumstances, the strike has curtailed the full range of SAR services. We are thus hindered in our efforts to fulfil our national and international commitments to provide safety services on a continuous basis. Our external trade depends on the provision of these services.
Many of the ships now in the St. Lawrence system are loaded with export grain. It is estimated that one million tonnes of grain must be shipped overseas from ports along the St. Lawrence from now to January, but the
Government Orders
Seaway must be open if our grain shipments are to be set apart.
Canadians rely on the St. Lawrence system for a variety of other commodities. General cargo and petroleum products are moved by ship to remote communities and major cities alike. An interrupted supply route will have negative impacts on the livelihood of many people. A reduction in the supply of raw materials carried on the seaway to our industries spells economic hardship.
During 1988 the St. Lawrence Seaway carried over 20 million tonnes of bulk cargo such as iron ore and coal to and from ports in the Great Lakes system. Over 15 million tonnes were also moved through the Seaway. A further 4.5 million tonnes of general cargo were also moved by this great waterway.
The economic significance of such figures is enormous. The seaway's yearly cargo throughput is in the order of 40 million tonnes. Some 60 per cent of the Seaway's traffic is shipped to and from overseas ports chiefly in Europe, the Middle East and Africa.
As of midnight, December 6, there were 51 ocean going vessels in the Great Lakes system west of St. Lambert lock. Of these, 33 are still above the Welland Canal. There are an additional 8 Canadian inland vessels per day requiring service. The average operating cost of these vessels varies from $5,000 to $25,000 per day and more, depending on the type of vessel. Many of the vessels face long delays. These delays will be longer if ice-breaker support is not available. Some ocean vessels may even be trapped in the system for the winter if ice-breaker assistance is not provided.
Should a number of the 51 ocean going vessels currently in the system be trapped, the losses incurred would be huge. Early system closure will also have a major impact on the viability of the Canadian inland fleet as it will be unable to meet all of its commitments.
With the outlook for below normal temperatures to continue for the remainder of December, the announced clearance date of December 19 may not be achievable and the dependability and reliability of the Seaway as a transportation route will be jeopardized. It is therefore critical that the Coast Guard services be restored as soon

December 8, 1989
Government Orders
as possible so that the seaway can be closed in an orderly fashion and all vessels can complete their transits.
In addition to the seaway, the St. Lawrence River ports have substantial impact on the local, regional and national economy. Traffic at Ports Canada facilities located on the St. Lawrence River generated over 16,500 jobs and $750 million in total income.
Let us look at the problem of ships currently delayed and the time lost. Today there were in excess of 70 ships experiencing delays in the St. Lawrence River below Montreal. In addition there were 51 ocean going vessels still to exit the St. Lawrence Seaway before its announced clearance on December 19.
This gives, in total, in excess of 120 ships affected or potentially affected if this strike is not immediately resolved. At an estimated daily cost per ship of from $5,000 to $20,000, the losses and ship time alone are presently about $1 million per day. This figure could escalate to millions per day if all the ships are not able to exit the seaway.
This strike has gone on for more than three weeks. Mediation talks began on November 26 and broke off three days later. We had hoped for a resolution on this labour dispute through mediation, but this strike which has gone on longer that we can tolerate has meant Canada has not been in the position to meet its national and international commitments to maritime safety.
I want people to note that we are not legislating a settlement to the issues that are involved in the strike. We are asking the workers to get back to their job so that they can carry on. They have an enviable record which is second to none. They are world class in their work. Nonetheless it has a tremendous impact on the Canadian economy as a whole.
More important, this bill calls for the establishment of two conciliation boards, one for either side of the equation. They will bring forth a settlement to the issue but we are not legislating the settlement per se. That is a very fundamental distinction.
We still want the unions to have the rights of the collective bargaining process, but there does not seem to be a possibility of that settlement right now between the union and management.
Nonetheless, we feel it is paramount for the shipping industry of Canada and for the economic well-being of the prairie grain system as the cargo flows through Thunder Bay and through the seaway system that the facilities and the efforts of the coast guard be put back into service so that we can be dependable and have a system that is working for the good of our country.

Mr. Speaker, it is ironic that I get up to speak today in opposition to this legislation. Today is the forty-first anniversary of the UN Declaration of Human Rights.
I strongly oppose this legislation and I want to outline the bad faith bargaining on the part of this government, which is the employer in this case. I would also like members on the other side of the House to understand the valuable contributions of the labour movement to our Canadian society.
The collective agreements for both the ship crews and the hospital services members of the Public Service Alliance of Canada expired in December 1987, two years ago. We are talking about the lives and the livelihoods of 3,600 people across this country.
In September 1989 the Federal Court rendered a decision that precluded Treasury Board from designating any of these members. For the first time all members of the hospital services and ship crews classification of the Public Service Alliance enjoyed the right to strike. Strikes commenced on November 11, 1989 for the ship crews members and on November 29, 1989 for the hospital service members. Emergency services were still being provided by the members of these unions. Ship crews suspended their strike on at least 10 occasions to respond to emergency search and rescue calls.
This is one of the many reasons why back to work legislation is terrible. These alliance members have shown themselves to be principled and responsible Canadians. That is more than can be said of this government. There is no reason to designate them as essential workers when they know when emergency services are needed, and they have demonstrated that.
The Federal Court obviously agrees that they like all other workers have the right to strike. They have the right to withdraw their labour. The right to strike, the right to withhold one's labour from a bad faith employer, is a fundamental right in our society. It is one of the most effective bargaining tools workers have in a society
December 8, 1989

where business has almost total economic control over many people's lives.
Along with destroying workers' right to strike, another reprehensible part of this legislation is the targeting of women workers as objects of contempt who do not deserve to be paid what they are worth. The majority of the federal hospital workers are women. They earn an average of $18,000 a year.
The key issue throughout the hospital workers' negotiations have been that of equitable pay. These workers have every right to expect restructured rates of pay and an economic increase reflecting the levels of the major economic indicators in Canada. These workers have experienced at least 10 years of pay inequity and have faced the refusal of the employer to address in any rational manner the issue of equitable rates of pay.
Instead the federal hospital workers were forced to file a complaint with the Canadian Human Rights Commission. They did so on September 9, 1981. The government delayed for almost six years before agreeing to an interim settlement in July 1987.
As I said earlier, it is ironic that this is the forty-first anniversary of the UN Declaration of Human Rights.
The consent order states:
The parties are agreed that the Hospital Services-Group, which
is predominantly female, has received less wages than the General
Services-Group, a predominantly male group, for performing work
of at least equal value.
The consent order lays out the method and terms for retroactive and future equal pay rates for the hospital service workers. The retroactive phase covered the periods from September 9,1980, to July 26,1987. On duly 26, 1987, the payments stopped. In November 1989 Treasury Board began to make retroactive payments for the period since July 1987 to the present.
These workers deserve more than haphazard retroactive payments for the money they earned long ago. They deserve the fair rates established in the pay equity settlement to be inscribed in the collective agreement. They deserve to see that money a week after they have earned it, not two years later.
The government is stubbornly refusing to be fair to these workers. The government is openly practising discrimination against women workers. Instead of nego-
Government Orders
tiating in good faith, establishing equitable rates of pay, entrenching the equal pay rates in the union contract, this government is forcing these workers who are on legal strike back to work.
I say abandon this legislation and just give these women the deal they deserve. The government is offering a settlement of between 4 per cent and 5 per cent. The difference in the rates of pay between this group and the general services group is estimated at more than 13 per cent. This issue will not go away by legislating unfairly treated workers back to work. It can only be addressed with a fair settlement.
All of this really comes as no surprise from a government whose own record on employment equity and pay equity is abysmal. The 1988 report of the Canadian Human Rights Commission specifically berated the government on the incredible delays in its study on pay equity in the public service.
The Employment Equity Act came into effect in 1986. It has been roundly criticized by labour, by women's groups, especially immigrant and visible minority women's groups, and by the New Democratic Party as having no teeth.
It is unfair to have to rely on the individual complaint process through the Canadian Human Rights Commission. The commission is not equipped to handle all of these complaints. We should establish and enforce employment and pay equity plans with goals and with timetables in a systematic way.
Some of the other outstanding issues for both the ships' crews and hospital workers negotiations are Article M-16, a no discrimination clause. The bargaining team wish family status and mental or physical disability to be added to the grounds of prohibited discrimination in the union agreement.
The union is asking for changes to Article M-21 of the contract. It wants its members to be able to partake of the new parental leave provisions of the UI Act. It is asking for 26 weeks of maternity leave.
We can compare this with what most workers in some western European countries have access to. In Sweden, women are eligible for nine months paid maternity leave and at a benefit level of 90 per cent of their earnings. They do not have to negotiate with a tight-fisted employer for a 26 week maternity leave.

December 8, 1989
Government Orders
In this case, the regressive Conservative government is also the employer. This government does not understand that policies that benefit workers also benefit the country. The government does not understand that progressive policies do contribute to a healthy economy. Tory economic policies such as the GST, the decimation of unemployment insurance and the constant attack on labour serve only to impoverish this country and to oppress working people.
The New Democratic Party has been enriched by the active participation of labour. When the Canadian labour movement and the CCF, the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation, joined together in the early 1960s to form a political party, a powerful force in Canadian politics emerged. Since then, labour has helped to guide the New Democratic Party to adopt the most progressive and sound economic policies of any elected political party in Canada.
Labour and the New Democratic Party have fought for medicare, unemployment insurance, maternity and parental leave, child care, collective bargaining rights, employment and pay equity. We have fought together for a better Canada, one not controlled by the rich few, a democratic Canada in which everyone has the economic and social resources to fully participate in Canadian life and Canadian society. We are committed to an economic strategy of full employment. We are committed to fairness for all working people, men and women.
In my riding, I consult with labour. Labour can always be relied on to come up with practical strategies to build a progressive Canada. Labour can always be relied on for energy and for a wholehearted commitment to bettering the situations of Canadian workers and the most disadvantaged of our society.
I am proud that the New Democratic Party is fighting for the rights of working people. Labour and the New Democratic Party are united against the unfair treatment of working people by this government. We are united in opposition to this back to work legislation.
I am also proud that our new leader, the hon. member for Yukon, is taking a strong leadership role on all of these issues, especially in opposing this back to work legislation. She is following in the footsteps of her predecessor, the hon. member for Oshawa.
We are a party and a movement that is united and forward looking. We put our common goals and our principles ahead of our individual differences. This government must bargain in good faith. It must not put back to work legislation into effect. I urge all members on both sides of this House to vote against this regressive legislation.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to join with my colleagues in this debate because of the very special significance that this concern that we are debating today in the House of Commons has for my riding at the west end of Montreal.
As many of my colleagues will know, the Ste. Anne's Veterans Hospital is an outstanding institution at the immediate western point of the Island of Montreal. It accommodates some 726 veterans, many of whom are in their final years, and is recognized in the community by the Legion groups which support it with their volunteer hours and by the many citizens who join with the professional staff to assist in providing services needed in caring for people in their final years.
Included in the Ste. Anne's Veterans Hospital are some 250 permanently bedridden patients. There are also some 400 who can move about in wheelchairs but who, without the assistance necessary to handle wheelchairs, are like the others, bedridden.
In the past days and weeks, my office has received calls expressing concern on behalf of families or volunteers having limited access to those needing care. All these people, my neighbours, electors in the riding of La-chine-Lac-Saint-Louis, electors in Vaudreuil to the west and Pierrefonds in the north, all are concerned about the health and care of the citizens in the hospital.
Patients with Alzheimers and dementia need routine in their life. If people change or meals are not regular, they become disoriented. It is a time when personal care and assistance is so vital to making life possible. All patients need care with bathing and shaving. Most need care with feeding.
One of the ladies who called my office and with whom I spoke expressed concern that regularity and meals for her family member was becoming very critical and that not receiving lunch until three or four in the afternoon is
December 8, 1989

having a negative effect on the well-being and health of these patients.
Those patients who need physiotherapy or psychological care are not receiving it. The absence of that care at this time in their lives carries with it without question a threat to their well-being.
The volunteers at the Ste. Anne's Veterans Hospital are themselves elderly, many of them senior citizens. Many are becoming very tired. They have been working long hours and extra time to fill in for the services that are normally rendered. It is difficult or awkward for them to cross picket lines.
The Ste. Anne's Veterans Hospital cannot function without its volunteer group. There are many hundreds who visit the hospital to assist the staff. The situation is now reaching a crisis point. Most staff members have been working hard, some of them for eight days straight on 12-hour shifts.
There was originally an evaluation of the work of the some 600-odd workers who service the hospital and it was determined that to keep it operating safely, operating with care, it would require that 90 per cent of the workers contribute. The offer that was made by the union to designate certain workers to assure essential services was 8 per cent of that number.
The seasonal events which are so much looked forward to at this time of year and enjoyed by all Canadian citizens will have to be cancelled at the hospital. Whether it is the music or whether it is the special food that comes with this holiday season, it becomes for those directly affected very much of an emergency.
A patient who is not able to receive physiotherapeutic treatment, perhaps for leg problems for some time, and is not able to walk on the wards, could be expected to suffer a major set-back to the point where he might never be able to walk again.
Negotiate then.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext:
I know that the negotiations are continuing. We have sat in this House of Commons listening to the reports of the minister that negotiations are ongoing. It is my hope that there will be a negotiation that will bring the workers back together. In the meantime, we have to concern ourselves with the well-being of the veterans. These are the people who actually represented
Government Orders
this country with the risk to their lives in the wars of the past.
During the strike, the physiotherapy department has had to be shut down. Another major impact on patients is the change in routine that makes older people nervous, especially when the change is beyond their control. The hospital is for many of them, at this stage in their lives, their home and it is the one area where they feel comfortable.
Quite a number of the Ste. Anne's patients cannot eat by themselves. They require spoon-feeding. If any of the members of this House have shared in the experience of a senior citizen in his or her last years, they will know how key to their happiness and to their good feeling of still being alive comes from having someone there to help and someone there to care. Volunteers are doing that job at the moment, but they are not trained to recognize, for example, the onset of choking. Nor are they trained to act upon the problems of a patient once he has experienced choking.
How can we balance these tremendous needs in our community? On the one hand, the patients should have our very best in service. At the same time, we must consider those who are anxious to share fairly in the distribution of resources of the country, the workers who make it happen.
I can add concerns of their cardiac patients who are becoming more and more anxious. This anxiety is brought on when meals are not served on time and when medication is not being given at the usual time. Daily activities are being rearranged and activity rooms are being changed. These are not big problems for most people, but are part of essential routine for some cardiac patients to whom anxiety can lead to fatality.

Mr. Speaker, the Department of Veterans Affairs runs a hospital and two veterans' homes. The hospital is located in Sainte-Anne-de-Bellevue, at the western tip of the Island of Montreal. There is the Rideau Veterans' Home in Ottawa and the veterans' home in Saskatoon.
I shall only talk about the situation in the Saint-Anne-de-Bellevue Hospital. The problem is most serious

December 8, 1989
Government Orders
there, mainly because the patients in that hospital need much more care than those in our two homes.

In the Ste. Anne's hospital, more than half of the staff belong to the hospital services group. While there are procedures in the event of a strike, the House will be aware that there were provisions that allowed designation of positions. This requires people in such positions to continue to perform their services if a strike is called. In this case, the essential service is to safeguard the health and security of the patients and to maintain their welfare.
The department did receive an offer from the union, but it was considered impossible to maintain the services on the basis of that offer. The response of the department indicated that while it was prepared to make an offer, the offer of 45 employees was well short of what was needed.
Now that the hospital at Ste. Anne's has been operating during the strike, it is important first to recognize that the strain on the employees did not begin when the strike started but had begun some considerable time in advance. Doctors, nurses and professional and support staff have been working 12 hour shifts. The nurses, in addition to their own work, have been doing the work normally undertaken by the higher levels of orderlies. The situation is becoming more and more critical.

Our doctor, nurses and other professional staff are working 12-hour shifts. In addition to their own duties, the nurses are doing the work normally done by the higher level assistants. The work of the other members of the hospital services group has been done in two ways: first, by the group of volunteers who usually help at that hospital.

It is an immense team of volunteers who contribute to the well-being of our veterans. In addition, they have moved some of the staff from other centres to try to assist. All have been working long hours and all are now, as might be expected, very tired.
I think we should pay tribute, and I am sure the House would wish to join me in doing so, to those who are keeping services available to our veterans and who have committed themselves to this end. Despite our best
efforts, the health and safety of the patients is coming into jeopardy and this has been noted over these past days.
The deputy minister, as reported by the minister in his report to the House on this matter, studied personally the situation in Ste. Anne de Bellevue and concluded that we have to act now because the health, safety and security of the patients is in danger. I believe that we have demonstrated why this situation cannot be allowed to continue any longer.

As I already told the veterans, my department considers its employees most important and wants to treat them fairly. I believe that the arrangements proposed in this legislation will allow an independent third party to help solve the dispute.
Our personnel is entitled to expect fair treatment. [English]
I would like to ask that the House respond rapidly to pass this legislation so that we may properly care for our veteran patients and look after those who did so much for us and are now unable to look after themselves. It is for this reason that I fully support the government's back-to-work legislation which is absolutely justified under the circumstances.

Mr. Speaker, I too am very pleased to rise in the House today to speak to Bill C-49, an act to provide for the resumption of certain government services.
I am pleased to speak to the bill but I am not so pleased about what the bill entails. In addition to this motion, the government has moved closure on this bill to cut off debate on this issue, something that I find absolutely appalling.
I believe there is no one more anxious to go back to work than the health services and the ships' crew workers. We all know that the work of these two groups provide an essential service to Canadians. These two groups of public servants have a long history of being ignored by the federal government, a history of pay inequity. The hospital workers went out on strike in the wee hours of November 30 and the ships' crew workers went out on November 13.
There are provisions in the Public Service Staff Relations Act which allow for the designation of essential personnel who are prohibited by law from going on strike during a labour dispute. However, nine government

departments failed to meet the deadline for submitting lists of personnel that they felt were essential.
The federal court ruled that the departments' mistake could not be overlooked and that these groups had the right to strike. As a result, all members of any of those groups were in a legal strike position if talks broke down. These groups have exercised that right. They are among the lowest paid in the federal Public Service. Is it any wonder that there are also the same groups that rejected the tentative agreement in March?
The major issues that led to the ships' crew group's rejection of a tentative agreement in March of this year were wages, hours of work, a sea duty allowance and wage parity on the east and west coasts. As of July 1987, wages on the west coast were behind private sector wages by 16 per cent and on the east coast wages lagged by 28 per cent. An east coast ship worker makes $2,000 less than his counterpart working for the same government on the west coast.
Given private sector wage increases over the past two years, these percentages are now much higher. The Public Service negotiators are not prepared to compromise any of the employees' requests in exchange for one benefit.
The members of this group work on the east and west coasts, on the Great Lakes and on the Canadian Coast Guard vessels, the fisheries vessels, search and rescue lifeboats, Public Works vessels and on Canadian forces auxiliary vessels providing support for naval vessels.
During the strike these federal employees have shown their good will and dedication by leaving the picket line whenever emergency services to the Canadian public were required. This to me indicates that these employees are dedicated to their jobs. They were dedicated when an emergency arose and they laid down their strikers' pickets and went back to work for those emergencies.
They are proposing, instead of higher pay scales, that they be given across-the-board sea allowances of $210 per month. The Department of National Defence already pays $177 per month to all personnel. The higher amount is because their pay scale is so much lower. The government could have settled this matter for $6 million. Considering how many days that they have been out on
Government Orders
strike, they could have saved this $6 million by preventing lost business during the strike period.
The hospital services workers have been on strike since November 30. I listened to the gentleman across the way from a riding in Montreal who spoke just before me and his whole speech was based on the veterans' homes in Ste. Anne de Bellevue and on the volunteers and how great it was that the volunteers were providing this much-needed service. Only briefly did I hear him refer to the workers, those workers who have been so dedicated to these veterans all these years, and those workers who too do not like to see those veterans not being cared for to the extent that they know that they themselves would care for them. I did not hear the hon. member address that.
On July 15, 1987, the Human Rights Commission Tribunal ruled that this group of people is undervalued and underpaid. When is the government going to recognize that? The tribunal's consent order called on the employer to compensate the workers for past discrimination, re-evaluate seamstresses and community health representative positions using the federal general services standard and to revise the health services classification standard to parallel.
The classification system was changed but only equalization payments were issued. No salary adjustments have been made.
This is not something that has gone on for a year or two, it has gone on for years. The Human Rights Commission has ruled that they are being discriminated against, that they are undervalued, that they are underpaid and the government is not recognizing this.
On average, the health services workers are entitled to an additional $3,000 a year. Given that their salaries are as low as $16,000 and average about $22,000, this is a significant amount and a disgraceful wage.
Health services workers offered to provide emergency services but the government would not come to an agreement with them, thinking they could provide services with military personnel and volunteers. I kept hearing from the previous speaker about how these veterans were not being cared for and how these volunteers were overworked and how tired they were. Well, these public servants offered to do the job and they will

Government Orders
not let them do the job and they will not pay them for doing the job.
The bill orders back the ships' crews and the hospital services workers immediately to their jobs. It establishes penalties for failure to comply; $500 to $1,000 a day for an individual. Someone who is making $18,000 a year is going to have to pay $500 to $1,000 a day if he or she does not comply.
It is unfortunate that this government is making out that these workers are the irresponsible ones. It is this government that is irresponsible. It is not bargaining in good faith. If this were really a caring government, then it would bring these salaries into line and get how these ministers would like to live on wages of $18,000 and $22,000 a year. We come into this building every day and we see the limousines sitting there with the motors running to keep the chauffeurs warm. In the summer time we see the limousines sitting there with the motors running to keep the chauffeurs cool. It is probably costing $18,000 a year in gasoline to keep those limousines out there. And these people do not have the courage nor the strength of conviction to pay these workers what they are worth and get them back to work.
This is a disgraceful situation. We have our veterans in the Rideau Veterans' Home who deserve the best care that we can give them. This quality care is given by these dedicated employees. I beg this government, if it wants these people to go back to work and if it is going to legislate them back to work, to make the commitment that it will bring their pay into line with other workers and show that it is bargaining in good faith.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian marine aids to navigation system is one of the fundamental elements of marine safety in Canada. The system consists of both floating and fixed aids to navigation on the east and west coast and on our major inland waterways. In all, there are some 8,000 floating aids to navigation comprising buoys of various types and sizes, ranging from seven-tonne buoys to lighter smaller spar buoys. These floating aids are complemented by fixed or shore-based aids to navigation, including light stations, ranges and day marks. The larger floating buoys are complex pieces of equipment that carry radar reflectors, whistles, battery power
sources, lights, bells, and in some cases, radar transponders. These aids are marked and located in accordance with international conventions so that they are understood by the international marine community. The positioning of floating aids is carefully determined to take into consideration many factors such as channel configuration, local weather conditions, the presence of hazards and the local requirements of marine traffic.
Because of our Canadian climate it is normal practice for many lighted buoys to be removed from service at the end of the summer navigation season because they cannot withstand ice. In areas where navigation continues year around, in spite of the presence of ice, the summer buoys are removed and replaced by a limited number of winter spar buoys which are able to withstand severe ice action. In the St. Lawrence, lighted summer buoys are normally replaced by unlighted spars during the latter part of November. These spars do not provide the same level of service as the normal summer buoys. For example, it is most common on the St. Lawrence when the winter spars are set to restrict river traffic to daylight hours because of the absence of the lights on the buoys.
With the strike of ships crews, the Coast Guard's ability to bring in the summer buoys and, in some areas, to replace them with winter spars has been hampered. In the St. Lawrence, all buoys between Sept Isles and the Seaway normally would have been removed or replaced by this time, particularly with the present weather.
The situation which has developed in the St. Lawrence was entirely dependent on climatic conditions. In view of the severe and early winter weather this year, the summer buoys, beginning in the section between Quebec and Tadoussac, have become iced over. Others have capsized and some are partly submerged. With the accumulation and movement of surface ice, many of these buoys have also been dragged off position severely. Some have been dragged into the channel where they have become potential hazards. Some buoys have had anchor chains broken and some of these have actually floated free.
This situation is deteriorating upstream from Quebec, all the way up to the Seaway, with some 200 of the total 404 river buoys being iced over, off position and sometimes entirely extinguished. The safety of marine naviga-

tion was recognized by both the Canadian Coast Guard and the pilotage authorities. This has been compromised. It was for this reason that navigation on a section of the river was closed to traffic last Friday. As a result of the ongoing assessment of the safety of navigation, the lower section of the St. Lawrence was subsequently reopened to navigation on December 5 under restricted conditions.
The safety of marine navigation is a primary responsibility of this government. To let this situation continue is to risk an accident involving shipping on the St. Lawrence River. Such an incident could possibly result in the inability of all ships to clear the St. Lawrence Seaway above Montreal prior to the closing of navigation.
Because the aids-to-navigation system on the St. Lawrence is essential to marine safety, we must move immediately to remove any buoys that are potential hazards and to restore the system with winter spars so that traffic to and from Montreal can continue through the winter months. The current situation is most critical, given that a number of ocean-bound vessels remain in the St. Lawrence Seaway and must exit the system prior to the announced clearance date of the Seaway, which I understand to be December 19.
I would mention that critical situations also exist in other parts of the country, particularly off the Labrador coast where the Coast Guard maintains some 36 buoys that are normally lifted by this time of year. New Brunswick's Saint John River, now frozen over, holds some 27 buoys which normally would have been removed in May and will now be lost or will be hazards to the navigation system in the spring.
This situation has gone on long enough. It cannot be permitted to continue to threaten the safety of navigation and, most important, the economy and financial well-being of Canada.
I know that when we get into a debate like this, there is always a question of individual rights versus the rights and responsibilities of the Government of Canada. I believe that it is the responsibility of the Government of Canada to ensure safety in shipping. For that reason, I
Government Orders
think we have to move in the direction that we are moving. We are doing it for the good of the country.
We are talking about balancing rights in this House on almost a continual basis. This debate today is no different. It is something like the abortion debate in a sense; a balance between the rights of the mother and the rights of the unborn. I think in this debate the rights of Canadians to ensure the safety of their navigation is of prime importance. When the negotiation process breaks down we are all losers in a sense. We hate to see it happen but from time to time in a democracy it does happen. That is what this debate is about today. It has been a long day. It has been a long couple of days in this House. But I believe that we are doing what is right for Canada. We are doing what is right for navigation.
In conclusion, I would simply reinforce the fact that the Canadian government has a responsibility to move quickly. I believe we are doing the right thing for the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, After the series of articles that appeared in the press about this strike, which is clearly legal, after talking to some of the strikers living in the riding of Gatineau-La Lievre, who told me about their concerns and what they consider to be unfair-Obviously, I read the documentation. If I may be allowed to quote, I read a decision that came the PSAC, which said that the federal government's decision to introduce legislation ordering federal public service employees in the ship's crews and hospital services groups to end their legal strike constitutes unjustified abuse of legislative powers.
However, I would not go as far as to say that. I think that what we see here is negligence, when we consider the position of these workers, whether they are on ships or in hospitals.
During the three and half weeks they have been on strike, members of the hospital services and ship's crews groups made sure that public safety was never at risk by always providing essential services. Consequently, it is clear that this bill contravenes the international conventions on freedom of association ratified by that same Canadian government.

Government Orders

If you may permit me, there have been so many articles and so many declarations on this issue it is obvious that the whole issue gets cloudier as each day goes by. The strike continues and we want to put an end to it because we realize it has ramifications, not only for the hospitals, for our ships but for security on the St. Lawrence and elsewhere.
Another person involved in this strike is a representative of the workers. Instead of negotiating a contract for the workers, the government is spending it seems hundreds of thousands of dollars of taxpayers' money. It would make more sense to have the employer sit down to negotiate a settlement with the employees, ratify it with the union and get things back to normal.
