When you consider that the Human Rights Commission, not last week or three weeks ago but over two and a half years ago, declared that these men were underpaid, it seems to me that knowing this issue would come to a head that sooner or later the President of the Treasury Board could expect that these men would be in a legal position to strike, which they are, and the whole thing would come to the surface.
If there is anything that governments do, it is to be sure that everything is done equitably; equal pay for equal work. This could be an anomaly, some kind of an exception that could have been overlooked, if we can use the term. We will give them the benefit of the doubt. But two and a half years after the Human Rights Commission declaration which is an independent body respected by everyone, it seems that that should have been the signal or cue to the government to say: "Let us go by the principle of equal work for equal pay, and sit down to negotiate a contract that will stand up to any rigorous examination, be it by the workers or their union". But that is not the case here.
We have had disputes and all kinds of excuses over the past few weeks. The problem is it is not the last three weeks of the strike. It is the fact that it is has been dragging on for two and a half years. Maybe this is unfortunately an aspect of government, that it constantly hedges on time. There is an expression in French that says: "Tout ce qui traine se salit. Evidemment.", and this is the case. Tout ce qui traine se salit. Evidemment. What was rather interesting to me was my Liberal colleague from Ottawa who wrote a letter of nearly two pages to the
President of the Treasury Board and concluded with the following paragraph:
I again assure of my strong commitment to the implementation of equal pay for work of equal value and ask for your support in helping our public to understand what can be a complex and lengthy process to implement.
Like I said, we will give them the benefit of the doubt. There is no doubt that it is a complex and limiting process to implement. But it has been two and a half years. We are not dealing with thousands upon thousands of employees, we are dealing with a group who, for some time, were 26 per cent behind in pay compared with the private sector. Some workers, paid by this government, are 16 per cent behind.
For example, those who are responsible for the maintenance of the Parliament Buildings are paid 16 per cent more. It is not that they are being paid more. They are paid for work, which is justifiable. But here we have the same employees in another part of the country doing important work in our hospitals getting 16 per cent less.

Madam Speaker, we could, of course, go on indefinitely about this issue and invoke all kinds of principles. I listened to the hon. member from the Quebec City area, I don't remember his riding, who spoke very well and very sensibly, but we cannot avoid the facts. It doesn't take a university degree to realize that the problem has been around for two and half years. It was bound to come to a head, and it was bound to end in a strike. Of course there was going to be strike. They said that after waiting for two and half years, they were not going to wait anymore.
The government had plenty of time. There was no problem from that point of view. However it was the kind of negligence that we see all too often. I am not saying that the present government, the Progressive Conservative Party, is more to blame than anyone else. That is not the point. I think that the problem is that the government underestimated the will and determination of the people who work in our hospitals, and who know theirs is an essential service, and as so often happens, our governments tend to think that these people are very conscientious and that the chances of their going on strike are minimal. However, after two and half years, especially considering the support they got from agencies like the Human Rights Commission, they knew some-
December 8, 1989

thing had to give. In fact, it is surprising that it took two and half years.
So I believe that under the circumstances we cannot- In their letter they ask that we understand the complexity of the issue. Quite so, but how can we defend the government's position when we know there has been enough negligence to trigger a strike. The workers walk off the job and obviously the government, faced with a situation it has ignored for two years, is unable to settle the issue once and for all in two or three weeks. So it introduces special legislation-I have seen some in the past-to force them back to work, promising it will negotiate in good faith. But I maintain that after so many years the employees are in a good position and their strike is justified. It is unfortunate to realize that some essential services might be curtailed, but I do not believe that such is the case. But we have to admit that the government is guilty of negligence in this case. It is as simple as that. Never mind the statistics and the various statements, practically anything can be justified, but still we have to acknowledge the fact that the President of the Treasury Board has indeed been very negligent.
Of course we cannot support them on this issue, but at least we can tell them we hope this is the last time we see a government-which can afford to do much better- bring in special legislation to order back to work a group of people who are underpaid when compared with colleagues doing the same job, a fact which has been proved by all organizations. Basically, the way I look at this problem, and I want to put this a simply as possible, is that I am convinced the government will order them back to work. However, as I read the last paragraph of the statement made by the President of the Treasury Board, I believe there will be a final meaningful negotiation to do justice to these men, the kind of justice they have not seen in years.

Mr. Speaker, in a way I am very sad to be participating in this debate today. I am also sad from the perspective of producers in my riding, farmers who
Government Orders
depend on the system to export grain to market. This is their livelihood.
But I am also glad because it will give members and myself an opportunity to talk about what is wrong with the system that permits these sorts of stoppages and what we should be trying to do collectively to make a better system for the future.
I come from a riding on the prairies which is approximately 25,000 square miles in area and which is almost entirely dependent on agriculture. Indeed, agriculture produces, even now some 16 per cent of the gross domestic product of the province of Saskatchewan. It is quite clear that neither Saskatchewan nor, I suggest, Canada can long continue to endure these sorts of work interruptions. I am trying to be as non-partisan as possible in saying this because I am not anti-labour and not anti-management. I think what I am anti is this sort of senseless system we have which permits stoppages of work that do less damage to the parties than to the nation as a whole causing immense problems for third parties whether it be farmers, whether it be students, you name it.
Whenever the system of collective bargaining breaks down, the safety valve mechanism that we have dates back to the Stone Ages. We live in a modem, sophisticated society. We are capable of putting men into space. We are capable of transplanting organs. Messages can go around the world in the twinkle of an eye through sophisticated telecommunication systems. We live in a modem, sophisticated society and yet our dispute settlement mechanism is one which goes back, surely, to the days of the cave man.
When the system breaks down, it is time for the parties to start slugging each other on the forehead with rocks until one or the other falls down or, as is most often the case, it is time to come crawling into the House of Commons for some back to work legislation. Clearly things should change.
First I would like to talk about this particular bill from the perspective of prairie agriculture, then from the over-all perspective of labour relations generally. I will try to make what I believe to be a constructive suggestion. I think we all know that Canada has a mammoth handling and transportation system which moves grain from the prairies to market. The well-being of much of

December 8, 1989
Government Orders
western Canada hinges on the continuing flow of this grain, particularly wheat, through the system of rail, river, road, canal and sea to purchasers throughout the world.
I am told that there are some 37 unions involved in the handling of grain between the farm gate and the port. They are involved in the country elevators, the railways and the grain terminals, the seaway, the St. Lawrence, the various ports, and they represent all sorts of individuals and occupations: grain handlers, grain trimmers, grain inspectors, weighers and samplers, seaway workers, lake carrier deck hands, mates and engineers, port stevedores, longshoremen, pilots, tugboat operators, railway trainmen, locomotive engineers, non-op shop craft workers, rail traffic controllers, various country elevator and grain service union personnel. There is a considerable number of employees and a considerable number of employers as well-the grain companies, railway, seaway, port authorities and so on.
Any one of these groups, at any given time, represents a vital link in the chain that is capable of breaking down and curtailing really remains the lifeblood of the southern prairies.
Canada exports more than 80 per cent of its wheat crop. Canada enjoys her reputation as a reliable supplier to the world of high quality wheat. The Canadian Wheat Board, which this government supports fully as the sole marketing agency for prairie export wheat, has been doing a good job maintaining and even expanding Canada's share of the world market in the face of unfair and cut-throat foreign competition.
The European Economic Community and the United States are both offering substantial export enhancement bonuses in order to maintain their share of market. These programs seriously undermine world grain prices, and this, in turn, has had devastating effects on our country which is so heavily dependent on exports. The Common Market has some 330 million people to draw from as a domestic population. The United States has some 250 million people. We in Canada have about 26 million people and so we are doubly dependent on export. We export a far greater share of our product than any of the other major wheat growing areas and, in turn, we have a much smaller domestic population to be able to match support programs.
Clearly it is a buyer's market out there. The importing countries value the quality of Canada's wheat but they can buy wheat elsewhere. The buyers do not have to put up with uncertainty of supply and delays in delivery. So when interruptions occur in our grain handling and transportation system, causing Canada to be unable to meet its obligations, other grain exporting countries will. Indeed, even the threat of labour-management induced interruptions in grain movement could lead to lost sales.
The Canadian Wheat Board, in effect, has to sell wheat to make sandwiches. The wheat has to be there to make tomorrow's bread. The nature of the business is that importers require large quantities on short notice and if the product is not on the shelf then it is simply not going to be sold. Canadian Wheat Board Commissioner Kristiansen, speaking of another work stoppage a couple of years ago, said that the stoppages at Thunder Bay had resulted in a million tonnes in lost sales. He is further quoted as saying:
As things drag out longer you lose more. There is no question in our
minds that we lost sales and substantial sales.
The major cost of these interruptions is lost sales opportunities. Other costs involve demurrage and the back-up following the stoppage, as well as additional rail costs in the case of seaway closures. Given the past history of stoppages in this country I suggest that this legislation is absolutely necessary. I will later suggest that we come up with measures in this House which would deal not just with this problem but with all similar problems so that there will not be the necessity to keep coming back here to resolve problems for which there should be a modem up-to-date mechanism.
I do not believe for a moment that there is anything to be gained by adhering to this status quo, this business of either side bashing the other on the forehead until one drops and there is some sort of a settlement. Meanwhile, there are people out of work, there is grain backed up, there is misery being inflicted in the country. It is archaic; it is antiquated; it does not make any sense in our society today.
I have been disappointed to say the least with some of my colleagues in this House who tell two stories. They go home to the prairies and tell the farmers that they are 100 per cent behind them and that this government is terrible and does not pay attention to agriculture, and yet they come back to Ottawa with a different story. Then it is time for them to start kowtowing to the big union bosses and saying: "Yes, sir, Mr. Bean" or "Yes, Shirley,

December 8, 1989

whatever you want that will be the way it is". There is one story told on the prairies and then the farmers are stabbed in the back by those same people down here in Ottawa.
I think prairie producers are wise to this sort of tactic. They are getting sick and tired of it. I suggest that colleagues across the way in opposition would be well advised to co-operate in the passage of this bill.
I would in a way dare them to keep it going until Monday and Tuesday when we have the agri-food conference here in Ottawa. They will have the opportunity to hear first hand from producers and those involved in the industry right across Canada. They will tell them how they feel about the stupidity of delaying and continuing to filibuster this sort of measure.
Same old Tory philosophy. It is a shameful travesty.

Mr. Speaker, we are hearing some interruptions of course from our colleagues in the NDP who like to hand it out but are of course are incapable of receiving anything. The difficulty with the simpering pantywaists who are sitting across the way is that they are too, too dependent on the apron strings of organized labour.
As a matter of fact, since we have been so rudely interrupted here by my NDP colleagues, I have to draw the attention of the House to a form letter from one Daryl Bean of the Public Service Alliance of Canada dated December 6, 1989. "Dear Member of Parliament," he states. He goes on to state that we are going to be asked to pass some back to work legislation. He points out that both groups provide services of enormous social and economic importance to the nation.
There is no argument there. Mr. Bean is right on. He is back. He is fresh from his bit part in "Saturday Afternoon Live" in Winnipeg which, as an aside, was really a marvellous spectacle for the nation to observe.
On the second page of this letter that Mr. Bean directs to members of Parliament, he goes on to get the old class knife in here. He states: "Could it be that some ice in the
Government Orders
seaway is causing economic pain to the friends of the government in corporate Canada?"
It seems to me that this has been going on now for some four weeks. Indeed there is important work to be done by these people. As Mr. Bean says, they provide services of enormous social and economic importance to the nation. I would think that four weeks of work stoppage is adequate. I would suggest that it is more than time for people to get back to work.
If Mr. Bean really means what he says on page one, he should be very pleased to see legislation such as this which recognizes that importance. I would urge all members to co-operate in passing this legislation as quickly as possible and getting these people back to work.
What is there to do in regard to the problem generally? I have been in this House for five years, and measures such as this have become annual exercises. Here we are now dealing with legislation in regard to the Seaway. Last year it was the Prince Rupert grain handling situation. The year before it was the Postal Services Continuation Act. The year before that it was the Maintenance of Railway Operations Act. We came back in the summer for that. The year before it was the Maintenance of Ports Operation Act. This has been the case all the way along. There is a long list of back to work legislation that had to be passed.
It is clear that the system is not functioning as it should. As I indicated earlier, we have a modern, sophisticated sort of society. Why is it that in the area of labour relations when the collective bargaining process breaks down it is necessary to have a work stoppage? Whether it is on the part of management or on the part of labour, I do not care. It is debilitating for all concerned. It is an embarrassment to the country. There is a great cost to various classes of Canadian people, generally those who can least afford it. In the particular case at hand it is prairie farmers who will bear the brunt of this thing. It is on their behalf that I urge members opposite to co-operate in this particular piece of legislation.
Over all, I say again that this is not a case of being pro-labour, anti-labour, pro-business or anything else. It is a case of wanting to be anti-stupidity. Our failure in our modern society to come forward with some better

Government Orders
way of resolving these impasses in the collective bargaining process is unforgivable. We have to do better.
This is a sort of abrupt cutting off. Hurtful, harmful measures inflicted upon people can cause damage, risk lives, costs innocent third parties considerable inconvenience and costs, cause embarrassment to our nation, threaten our markets and our reliability as a supplier. All these things point again and again to the need to do something better.
It is in that light and with that sentiment that I again make an appeal to this House, as indeed I have done through four or five private members' initiatives past and present, to try to work toward finding a better dispute settlement mechanism, some manner in which we can resolve these disputes before they get to this harmful, hurtful stage.
I do not pretend to know what the answer is, but it seems to me that we could form an all-party committee. Members from all sides of this House could hear evidence, could see what is being done in other countries. It may be a two-envelope system or it might be some form of court. There are specialty courts in some countries. There is the admiralty. There are obviously courts which specialize in matrimonial matters and probate matters. Why not in the resolution of labour disputes?
The collective bargaining process is good. It has to be there, clearly. There is no question about that. But let us have a better way of trying to resolve the breakdowns when they come, because the human cost and the dollar cost to our country are simply too great.
In regard to this particular bill I urge members on all sides to give speedy passage to the legislation in order to stop the terrible damage occurring to Canada's grain sector, to help out prairie agriculture and to help out farmers who are being beset by real difficulties in world export markets.
Over all, in regard to the big picture in terms of labour disputes generally-not just this one, but all of the other ones which have occurred and which we see in here year after year after year-I again say: let us look upon it from an all-party point of view. Let us try to get together to find some new mechanism to deal with it. I do not know what the answer is, but I think we have to get together. Surely collectively we can come up with something. We
live in a modern society. There is a lot of talent in here. Clearly there is a need which must be addressed.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in this House this afternoon to oppose this bill and oppose it strenuously.
This piece of legislation tries to deal with three fundamental points. First, it talks about pay equity between men and women, between the east and west coasts and it deals with equity between private and public labour. The government has brought this bill in because it has failed to live up to its commitments to bring in pay equity. That is one of the points which I will come back to later.
The second point that this bill is dealing with is the whole question of labour rights. It is part of a Tory government program to undermine systematically the rights of labour in this country. Workers have won the right to organize and to bargain collectively. They have won the right to work or to withhold their work. This bill is part of an agenda to undermine this right.
It is always comical to listen to the Tories at a time when the eastern bloc countries are recognizing as a part of fundamental democracy that one must allow workers the right to collective bargaining and the right to strike. Even the eastern bloc countries are now recognizing this. Yet the Conservatives are going in the opposite direction.
The third thing that this bill shows is the incompetence and bungling of this government. This is a result of total incompetence. Is this not part of a Tory agenda? I sit here bewildered, wondering why they are not willing to settle. It is going to cost $6 million. What is behind it? Why will they not give workers the rights and the money they deserve? It is a measly amount of money.
I begin to ask myself: What ulterior motives do the Tories have? Why are they being so hard-nosed about this? You begin to wonder if it because John Crow has said: "If you give these workers fair wages, with the GST coming in next year there is going to be a push for additional wage increases in the public sector and the inflation rate will go up". Is this not part of their GST package?
Much of this has to do with the lack of the government's fairness with its employees, particularly hospital workers. I have worked in long-term care. I have worked with veterans, particularly elderly veterans. Hospital workers form one of the hardest working groups you will ever get. It is difficult working with seniors. These are

dedicated people. They provide care and nurturing. They provide a whole range of services that must be recognized. Yet, in this case, there is a yawning gap between the fine words of the government and the meagre actions that have been taken at the ministerial level.
Let us listen to the fine words of the Prime Minister when he was debating the leader of the NDP in the 1988 election campaign on pay equity. The NDP leader said: "In this area of pay equity in which you have direct responsibility, you made a commitment in 1984 in terms of narrowing the gap between men and women. Why did you not act?"
The Prime Minister's explanation was: "Because we did. We passed the Employment Equity Act that Flora McDonald was responsible for in the first case. Second, we have the joint union-management committee to implement pay equity in the Public Service that is now going on to Treasury Board under Pat Carney, with all of our unions, where we are agreeing on a policy of pay equity for women for equal pay. This is what has been going on. This is the hard work that is going to produce, I think, quite remarkable results that will meet the objectives we both seek".
Those are nice words but nothing has happened. The Prime Minister is saying "a policy of pay equity for women". Why does he not implement it?
In the case of hospital workers they have been fighting for equity since 1981 and have argued successfully that their work was fully comparable to higher paid general service government workers. Finally in 1987 there was an interim consent order to give these workers $28 million. This was to be followed by job classification changes in a final settlement.
But the government has not kept its word. It has not kept its word on changing classification and pay scale. Instead, it has proposed a token payment as an attempt at compensation. The principle is not token, nor is the amount of money. These people are entitled to a full rate of pay of nearly $3,000 a year more than they are now earning. Their earnings are among the lowest in the Public Service, anywhere from $16,000 to $20,000 a year. That is not even what the members over there get for their tax free allowance, and they are expecting working

women, many of them sole bread winners, to support their families on that.
Let us go back to the fine words of the Prime Minister in response to the leader of the NDP. Let us realize that they were spoken on national television during the leaders' debate. Surely this is as close to another one of the Prime Minister's famous declarations concerning a sacred trust.
What did the Prime Minister say? First, the leader of the New Democratic Party said: "But the gap has been widening, not narrowing. The gap between men and women, since you have been Prime Minister, in the Public Service has been widening, not narrowing. Again you say that you have legislation here that is right. It has been passed. You could run off a nice little list saying that we have passed this, that we have done this, but unless it is followed up by administrative actions to bring about fairness and equity it means nothing".
The Prime Minister's response was: "Mr. Broadbent, I am trying to explain to you that this is precisely what we have done. This is being done by the Treasury Board as the representative of the employers of all Public Service unions to work out with the unions in a mutually safisfactoiy manner a program that will give rise to exactly equality".
Listen to this: "We are budgeting for funds required on an ongoing basis to make sure they are available so that this money will be given to those women who have been deprived of the degree of equity that we seek". That is what the Prime Minister said.
I will repeat that. He said, "We are budgeting for funds required on an ongoing basis to make sure they are available so that this money will be given to those women who have been deprived of the degree of equity that we seek". That is very nice for him to say during an election campaign, but it is so typical as happens with the Prime Minister. Once the election is over he forgets all about it.
What has happened then? The Prime Minister was talking as though there was an inevitability, that there would be pay equity. Have the workers been given the amount due to them? No. Has the government conceded their case as to classification and salary? No. Has the government even recognized that it is paying in some

cases below poverty level wages? No. In all of these things this is what the dispute is about.
Before I go on to labour aspects I wish to deal with the whole question of the people working in the coast guard, the ships' crews. I had a letter faxed to me today from one of my constituents concerning this legislation. I want to read it because it states succinctly what is involved here. It is addressed to myself and reads;
I am writing you to register my extreme dissatisfaction with the manner in which the Treasury Board has conducted negotiations with the men and women belonging to the Public Service Alliance of Canada, (Ships' Crews). I feel the Treasury Board has not bargained in good faith, indeed they have hardly bargained at all.
Please consider: That after 2 years without an agreement, the PSAC members (ships' crews), out of repeated disappointment and frustration, has engaged in a legal strike with their employer; that the Ships' Crews provide search and rescue functions, on both coasts of Canada, in addition to maintainence and supply services of the Canadian Coast Guards; please consider also that the union and the crewmen themselves, at the outset of the strike, agreed unilaterally to maintain vessel response capability in the event of a marine distress. This has been done. During the course of the strike there have been several instances where striking crew members have responded to emergency distress calls or co-operated in the handling of emergency situations such as the recent oil spill and resultant fouled beaches near Sooke, B.C.
If the Treasury Board is unable to conclude an agreement after 2 years, I submit it is either government policy to delay the implementation of a new agreement or indicative of ineptitude on the part of the Treasury Board. It certainly isn't due to unreasonable wage demands, as a comparison with comparable jobs and duties within the federal, provincial, and civic public services will show. In the event of either government policy or ineptitutde of the Treasury Board, the situation is wrong and should be corrected.
As employees of the federal government, these "-Brave and dedicated men and women - " (Minister of Transport, the Hon. Benoit Bouchard, in Hansard, October 16, 1989), to whom the House of Commons recently paid tribute, deserve better treatment from the Treasury Board. As Canadian citizens they have a right to believe that their government will treat them fairly and justly.
After having engaged in a legal strike, as a means of last resort, and after having conducted themselves in a responsible manner consistent with the finest traditions of seamen and democratic trade unionists and citizens, the government has proposed legislation to force these men and women back to work.
This is akin to moving the goal posts in the middle of the game. I urge you to vigorously oppose this forthcoming legislation and I further urge you to apply as much pressure as you can to the Treasury Board to end this dispute, by proper negotiation, in a fair and just manner, not by force of legislation.
I think that sums up a great deal of what is taking place in this House. What we now have is the Tory agenda to undermine the rights of workers in Canada.
I just want to recall a story about my father when he emigrated to this country. He arrived in Edmonton in March and he, like many other men, sought work. Most of the work available was manual labour. At that time there was a need for ditch diggers. The way the ditch diggers were hired was that the boss would put out 100 shovels and the men fought for the shovels. If you got a shovel, you dug and you worked. If you could not fight and get a shovel, there was no work.
Then they put the biggest man up at the top of the ditch. If he dug 10 feet, you dug 10 feet, because if you did not there was another man there to take your place.
It was because of these kinds of working conditions that my father was involved in some of the first organizations of trade unions in this country. I see, systematically, right wing governments like the Vander Zalm government in British Columbia and this Tory government, trying to return labour's rights and workers' conditions to those of pre-World War I.
Labour law in Canada is usually statutory law in which collective agreements between workers and management are worked out under the auspices of labour codes, labour standards and other legislation. Yet it should not be forgotten that the freedom of association is a hard won freedom which has a long and honourable history, both here and in the United Kingdom where much of the fight for labour recognition began.
This freedom of association was recognized-some would say imperfectly-in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms in 1981. Canada has further ratified international covenants recognizing collective bargaining. It is a member of the International Labour Organization which among its roles serves as an international watch-dog on
December 8, 1989

labour practices of members. It has been disturbing to many of us to see Canada, in the eyes of the ILO, turn from an international innovator to an international violator.
Unfortunately the truth has been that punitive and coercive legislation of several provincial governments and the federal government has brought the International Labour Organization's rebukes. The most recent case involved the federal government itself and its Bill C-68, the Postal Services Continuation Act in 1987.
Not only is there an attack on labour through direct legislation, but many of the other programs introduced by this government are intended to undermine the position of labour. Examples of this are the erosion of the Unemployment Insurance Act, to make it more difficult for people to receive unemployment; the continuation of a high unemployment rate which forces workers to accept underpaid jobs; and the harmonization of wages in Canada with the United States forced by free trade.
Yesterday I was at a committee meeting in regard to truck leasing companies. These are the companies that lease the big rigs and large trucks to truckers and do their servicing in Canada. Their representatives appeared before the committee. These companies are saying that now with the free trade deal it will be cheaper for them to establish their shops across the line and then lease back into Canada these large trucks.
The attack on labour legislation comes with such things as this high-handed piece of legislation that has been brought in by the very government which refuses to bargain in good faith.
If you ever want to see an inherent conflict of interest in labour-union management negotiations, it is when management has also got the power to legislate people back to work. Then they simply sit back and say: "We don't need to bargain in good faith because when the chips are down we will force the workers back to work."
It is also interesting to take a look at the timing of this back to work legislation. The strike has been going on for some time. The employees have acted responsibly. There has only been action by the government when its friends, the big shipping companies, start to get antsy that they are losing money, that they start to be concerned that they are going to lose income. Yes, they are.

It is so silly. Their loss of income is significant to this government, but the equity and fairness to the workers does not appear to be.
You wonder about the Prime Minister and how he is able to say that he is a self-proclaimed friend of the working man. Yet what does he do? He certainly does not believe in the rights of labour to organize, to bargain and to negotiate a fair and equitable contract. He certainly does not believe in the rights of women to pay equity and equal pay for work of equal value.
I am proud to be part of the New Democratic Party. I am proud of our alliance with labour. I am proud of the fact that I also have a union background and have been involved in a variety of unions from the steelworkers, to mine mill, to CUPE.
A fundamental part of a democracy is based on the freedom of workers to organize, to bargain for fair wages and to work with other people like the New Democrats for fairness not only in the workplace but for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, let me say at the outset how well the chair becomes you. It is nice to see you back in your seat.
I have watched the individual presentations on this very serious subject since the outset. I think it is safe to say that I have seen practically every speaker. I put myself in the position of members of the public who have watched the debate. I think there is certainly a risk that some people may be confused about what precisely is going on here. Quite frankly, I don't blame them. It is difficult to understand.
We have a situation here in which people who do a great service for Canada and who, in the opinion of certainly this side of the House, are seeking what is at least a minimum fair compensation are being told: "We have not the time to discuss the problems with you. We are going to legislate you back to work."
I have never belonged to a union and I have not been involved in these kinds of activities. I think, however, there is a logic here that one has to look at. At least from the perspective of where I sit and the perspective of where I have been for the last 30-odd years, I wish to try to put some kind of a sense into what it is we are doing here on a Friday afternoon.

I would like to begin by giving a recount of some of the maritime activities that Canada is involved in and what things maritime mean to this country. I would like to go on and have a look in a little more detail at what this bill does. I would like to have a look at what it does and to whom. Then I would like to be able to give you, Mr. Speaker, some of the ideas that I have on the question of whether it is right or whether it is wrong, in my opinion and in the opinion of many of my colleagues on this side of the House.
We tend to forget from time to time but those of us in Atlantic Canada are constantly reminded of the great maritime country in which we live. Canada is a great maritime country. We also have extensive maritime interests and substantial maritime obligations to go along with that.
I would like to quote some figures. To begin, we border on three of the world's largest oceans. We have the largest coastline in the world, 250,000 kilometres, the second largest continental shelf and our economic zone is so large that it covers about 8 million square kilometres in the three contiguous oceans. That is nearly equal to our land mass of about 10 million square kilometres.
Our continental shelf is rich in oil, natural gas and other exploitable mineral resources. In addition, it is no news to Atlantic Canadians or Pacific Canadians, and I hope to all Canadians that large rich fishing grounds lie off both our coasts. Canada claims jurisdiction over them to a distance of 300 nautical miles now and we on this side of the House are hoping that in the future we will be claiming jurisdiction for a little bit outside the 200 miles, so we can put some order into what it is that happens and we can take control of our own resources.
Canada is the world's largest exporter of fish. One sometimes wonders if that is true by the importance the government gives to the fishing industry. I can assure all members that in the very near future when we talk about total allowable catches on the east coast of Canada off the coast of Newfoundland that it is going to get a profile here that this House hasn't seen in some time. I am certainly guaranteeing that those of us on this side of the House will make sure that that is so.
Our seaborne trade, which is what is involved here, has grown impressively in the last 20 years. As a major trading nation, Canada has to transport many of it products to western Europe and to and from several trading partners along the Pacific Rim, including Japan, which is a very large trading partner of ours.
Exports today represent 30 per cent of Canada's gross national product, making it the third most trade reliant nation in the industrialized world, and 35 per cent of these exports leave Canada by sea. Those exports include wheat, grain, oil. Bauxite and tin are, in addition to some of the strategic materials in the import field.
The last figures I had which I could quote with accuracy were in 1982 and our international seaboard shipping, both exports and imports, totalled approximately 200 million tonnes. That is a lot of shipping. The value of the deep sea portion of the water based trade, excluding the shipping to and from the United States, was $40 billion. To move these goods, to give you some indication of the volume, Mr Speaker, some 110 merchantmen and tankers enter and depart Canadian ports daily.
I want to look at the third ocean, the one that we tend to forget from time to time. Over the past two decades the strategic importance of the Canadian Arctic archipelago has been enhanced for a number of reasons. We have had the discovery of high grade mineral deposits and the development of technologies for their extraction and transport. In addition, the increase in commercial scientific military use of the Northwest Passage has kept the Canadian Arctic in the forefront and indeed has kept all of us in this House in debate on that subject from time to time.
Last, but certainly not least, the three oceans contribute vitally to Canada's security in that they separate our countiy from the territories of potential enemies.
That has given some indication of the maritime interests that we have in Canada. To say that they are vital is perhaps the understatement of the day.
Who are the people involved in making sure that these maritime interests continue to be served properly? This is not the time or the place to speak about Canada's navy, and I am hoping that there will be other occasions to do that.
December 8, 1989

It goes without further explanation. It is axiomatic that a country that has a maritime interest must also have personnel, services, measures and policies to make sure that these interests are properly served.
One of the things that we have been very proud of in this country is that we have always responded to the call of the sea, and I think I can say from personal experience and from the knowledge of my history of Canada's maritime heritage, we have done it well.
To quote you one example, and I do not think it would be out of place, I would remind this House that when World War II started, Canada's navy had 10 ships and 2,000 people. By the end of World War II, in something like 2,150 days, the Canadian navy was the third largest allied navy. It had 100,000 officers and men and it had close to 400 ships. If you work that out on the back of a cigarette package, it is around one ship every five days and about 50 men a day.
For my own case in my own province, less than two weeks ago I was honoured to have been the guest speaker with a group of Newfoundlanders called The First 200. They were the first 200 men who answered the call when the call for volunteers went out in Newfoundland in 1939. Within two months of World War II beginning, 200 men were on the Furness Withy jetty in St. John's, Newfoundland, to set sail to serve their country. I was delighted that a goodly number of them attended this meeting and they were as ready to go now, 50 years after the event, as they were when they were in their late teens and their early twenties.
This is one example of the kind of fortitude that our people who served Canada and our maritime needs have shown and will continue to show in the future.
Let me have a look at our auxiliary forces. I am talking now about the crews involved in this particular issue. We are talking about the coast guard. We are talking about the auxiliary forces that serve the Canadian navy. We are talking about fisheries and oceans and we are talking about certain elements of the research categories.
I say in modesty and with a certain amount of humility that I suspect that there are a few people in the House who have a real feeling for what it is that these men and women have to do. I have a real feeling because I have had the honour, the privilege, the duty and the responsibility of being a sailor at sea, all my life. I might add also that my family have followed this tradition for seven generations. I come from a fishing family. I come from a
Government Orders
family of seafarers. All my colleagues from Newfoundland have had personal experiences in the sea and with the sea. It is a heritage that we are very, very proud of. I know that I speak also for my colleagues from Atlantic Canada and from other parts of the west coast.
Let me try and paint a picture for you, Mr. Speaker. If it is a a normal situation, you proceed to sea on a Monday morning. If you are lucky you will have a reasonable sea and you will return to harbour with few difficulties. You are not in communication other than by radio with the rest of the world once the lines are slipped until you return to harbour. The captain of the ship is in his own way master of all he surveys and the ship's company, the team that makes up that crew, live a life and death situation from the time they leave until the time they get back.
Let me take an unusual situation. You may sail at any time and you may never return. I reluctantly make reference to a very sad occasion which I recall more vividly than I would like. In mid-October members of the coast guard rescue team went to rescue a diver in distress in a cove just outside St. John's, Newfoundland. Due to the nature of the elements, the crew of four, the coxswain and the crew of that fast response vessel, within view of the public essentially were lost at sea. In fact, their bodies have not been recovered. How do you portray that in the heat of a negotiation? How do you translate that to somebody, either in the highest court in the land, in this House, at a negotiation table, or in any other way, shape or form. It is very difficult.
As I stand and talk with my colleagues here today, I am told that there is a storm in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and around 250 kilometres off Prince Edward Island at least one ship is in dire straits and we fear that something even more difficult may have happened to another one. Eight metre seas, that is a 25-foot swell. Can you imagine launching a small craft in a 25-foot swell to carry out a rescue operation?
Well, Mr. Speaker, enough of the drama, but it is not meant to be drama. These people are on strike through a proper organization. It was deemed totally legal what they were doing. They would not let life and safety suffer. On many occasions they met the normal criteria, they laid down their pickets and placards and went to sea and, in some cases, carried out some of those rescues

Government Orders
that were attempted off Newfoundland that ended so tragically.
People who would do that I believe deserve something in return. I believe that they deserve in return more than an unprecedented action of legislating them back to work, an unprecedented action of closure to do this and an unprecedented action of rewarding those people who give of their time, energy, talents, heritage and, yes, their lives, with an order to go back to work and the inability to continue to negotiate for what is theirs, a fair settlement.
These people earn around $20,000 a year. These people I just discussed take home $240 a week. What are they asking for? They are asking for 50 cents an hour. Should we legislate them back to work for 50 cents an hour? I have no shame and I have absolutely no second thoughts about standing in this House today and going to bat for these people. I do not think they would expect anything else from anybody with a seafaring background, and I do not think they would expect anything else from a background of people who care, like my colleagues around me here today.
We are not asking for something unreasonable. Where I stand on this issue is not determined by where I stand on this side of the House. I feel strongly about this, I feel almost emotional about it and I believe that these people are not getting a fair shake. This is why I am speaking here today and if I were allowed to, Mr. Speaker, even with the great flexibility that you have allowed me in this House, I would go on as long as you would allow me, because I believe it is an issue that needs to be discussed and I hope I have the credibility to do that.

I have heard the figure of $2 million per day for the ships; I have heard the $6 million total that will make up the difference. Perhaps there is a principle involved on the other side of the House and with the President of the Treasury Board that we do not know about. If there is, could the next speaker please tell us? Will somebody let us know?
There is something that I do not understand about this. If it is as simple as the 50 cents that we are talking about, in return for the services that are provided by these brave men and women, then I cannot understand why we are here on a Friday afternoon and why somebody does not just go back to the table right away and negotiate. There is not a great deal of negotiation to be done. I think it is very fair.
There is another aspect that bothers me. I do not have evidence for this, but I find it passing strange that the hospital service workers for the veterans' hospitals are included in the same business. It was not too long ago that the hon. Minister of Veterans Affairs stood in this House and gave a very eloquent and excellent presentation as a tribute to the men and women who served this country. I believe there are still 144,000 veterans, many of whom are being cared for by the hospital service workers that are the subject of our debate here this afternoon.
From what I know about the issue, these workers are looking for parity. They were, according to the Human Rights Commission, at some point in time at least $34 million behind in what they were owed by an objective standard. That leads me to believe that perhaps what they are looking for is perhaps as fair as what our sailors are looking for. Equally, I have difficulty understanding why we cannot seem to be able to go back and bargain with them, because I think what they are asking for is equally fair.
I am told that the 144,000 veterans, or a number of them who are hospitalized, are receiving care. My colleague, the hon. member for Lachine-Lac-Saint-Louis described the circumstances at Ste. Anne de Bellevue. It is not in my riding, but I made it my business to be in contact with some of the people as part of my responsibility as critic for Veterans Affairs, and I was equally satisfied that, at some cost to the government, these services are being maintained. Therefore, what are we dealing with? We have a situation of dedicated people who are asking for fair treatment. We are not asking for
December 8, 1989

the world for them. In both the case of the ships' crews and the hospital services workers, their demands seem reasonable, and after less than two weeks' of negotiations, everything has come to a standstill.
The logic of this I find very difficult to understand. There will be a great disappointment when we stand in this House and vote on closure. It will be a great disappointment, I believe, for those people who are affected: 2,300 sailors and 1,300 hospital services workers. I think they will believe, and they have every reason to believe, that they have been let down.
I hope that in my small way I have made some contribution to those of us who are going to vote to try and convince them that in my heart of hearts and on this rare occasion, I must say, speaking totally apolitically, but speaking more as a sailor and as somebody who has been involved in this way of life for many years, I can honestly say that what they are asking for is fair and just and, I believe, quite frankly we owe it to them to go back and have another look.
If I had a closing remark, if I had a closing statement, I think I could convey the business of being a sailor and going to sea by quoting a remark made by Samuel Johnson a few hundred years ago. He said: "Should a man contrive to be in jail, he would never go to sea because being at sea is like being in jail with the chance of being drowned."
That is what we are dealing with, Mr. Speaker, and we need to respect that and do something just and real about it.
I thank you for your indulgence and I thank all my colleagues for their indulgence for the extra time.

Mr. Speaker, in some 21 and a half years in this place, this is the tenth or twelfth time I have been present dealing with back to work legislation.
I want to say at the outset, Sir, that the passing of such legislation has never been a sign of success by the government. It has been a sign of failure by the government on all those occasions. I will not deny that there will be a rare exception that would cause a national emergency or something like that when Parliament
Government Orders
probably unanimously would pass back to work legislation, but it is so rare as to be almost inconceivable.
I listened to speeches of spokesmen for the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Veterans Affairs yesterday and may I say something about the matter. As I recall, it was stated that in the realm of safety, security and emergencies this legislation was necessary.
Of course, the coast guard and the people in the onshore facilities guaranteed that they would be there in the event of an emergency, in the event of a requirement for search and rescue. On this very day they stood by their word and they did their job. Apparently two ships have been lost in the Gulf of St. Lawrence and tragically 39 lives may have been lost in the most horrible of conditions. Our search and rescue and coast guard people are still there trying to find survivors. I do not want to hear any more nonsense from government spokesmen about emergencies and search and rescue. The problem is that the Department of Transport is going to lose quite a few thousand dollars on buoys that should have been stored for the winter, but are going to be sunk by the ice.
I listened to the Minister of Veterans Affairs yesterday. He gave a good speech, particularly about what was happening at Ste. Anne de Bellevue. If it is that serious, how come it took this long to take action? I will tell you why it took this long. It was not until it cost the ship owners a couple of million bucks and they put some heat on the government that we got the legislation. Then and only then did it happen. If the government had been bargaining collectively, we would not have reached this impasse.
When you have a stupid or bad employer you are going to have a tough, mean union. It is inevitable. When you have a good conscientious employer, you have a good conscientious union and there is a minimum of difficulty. I have been through this too many times, both in this House and when I worked on the railroad. The deck is stacked. They play one group in society against the other.
PSAC put it very well today in its circular. When the hospital services group attempted to negotiate similar arrangements as the coast guard did regarding emergencies and providing a minimal number of staff, the government would not agree. I would like the Minister of Veterans Affairs to explain that. It was a negotiable item in the immediate term. Nothing happened. They go on to say, and I agree with them, that it was deliberate. The employer and the departments are preferring to pit

December 8, 1989
Government Orders
one vulnerable societal group against another, making hostages of aged people, the infirm, veterans and poorly paid hospital workers. In terms of being any kind of a manager, that is despicable. It is not good, sound, fair management.
These people have been two years without a contract and three years without a raise in pay. Nobody could say that they were impatient. They have been more than patient. That is a degree of tolerance that I doubt most of us would have. MPs automatically get 2 or 3 per cent every January and do not even have to bargain for it. It is laid on.
However, when there is a situation where employees go two years without a contract, three years without an increase, any government or any management, any bargainer on the government side who would think that these people are not going to fight for and demand to catch up are kidding themselves. If they refuse to recognize and face up to that, they are faced with a strike. Their solution is to fly in the face of every tenet of free collective bargaining. It is called stacking the deck, and the government holds the cards.
I have suggested to various unions for a number of years now that they should return to what John L. Lewis always did with the United Mine Workers. Six months before a contract expired they would submit their demands for the next contract. If a settlement had not been reached when the contract expired they went out on strike. His principle was no contract, no work.
These people have gone two years without a contract. There were instances when they have gone three years without one. I remember once, when I was in the railway, we went two years without a contract. When we had a strike, mostly over retroactive pay as well as the 40-hour week in 1950, it was a chief justice who told the government and the railroads where to head. We got retroactive pay and we got the 40-hour week. We had to shut down the whole country for 10 days and I can tell you the employees were the first ones not to enjoy it.
When you have a situation where management sits around on their hands for two years and there is no contract settlement then something is fundamentally wrong. I listened to the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek talking about the poor farmers. I think he mentioned a million tonnes of grain that is in the Great Lakes Seaway ports, the St. Lawrence ports and on board ships. My first point is that the whole western half of Saskatchewan, all of Alberta and the Peace River country in British Columbia ship their grain west, not east. So, none of the grain in the hon. member's constituency goes east. There might be the odd rare carload of malting barley or something. He was weeping tears for the farmers in his riding.
The point is, as the PSA said, here we have the government playing off one societal group against another. I have always been straight with my farmers and the trade union members in my riding. On countless occasions I have tried to put each side's case for argument to the other. Thanks to the Farmers' Union and the trade union movement there have been countless conferences on the prairies among fanners and workers to sort out the problems that they both have.
There is a principle here that gets continually ignored, not just by this present government but by the previous one too on several occasions. The principle is that when you have a collective agreement, management submits its proposals for the coming year, and the union, on behalf of the employees, does the same thing. I would not mind seeing something in the law that requires both sides to submit proposals at least 90 days and maybe six months before the expiration of a contract so they would be required to bargain.
I am not suggesting for one minute that there have not been occasions when the union has not been wrong. The union doesn't claim to be perfect, but in the overwhelming majority of cases in my experience it has always been management which had the economic power and the political influence, either by the government or from the government, to get its way. Today is another classic example of how any employer, but particularly this government as an employer, could sit back and watch its own lowest paid employees go three years without an * increase.
December 8, 1989

Now, I expect my friend from Fraser Valley to take that into consideration, the fine Christian gentleman that he is. It must twinge his conscience a little bit at least. I would like to think and hope that he went to people in the Department of Transport, the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Treasury Board and said that it is not right. I hope he has done that. If he has not, maybe he should, like an hour ago.
There has been a certain atmosphere here for the last several years when it came to collective bargaining no matter whether it was in the private sector or between the government and the employees. But have you not noticed and remarked, Mr. Speaker, that in the last few years most of it has been between the government and its employees.
A remarkably high degree of settlements are reached between the trade union movement and the employers in the private sector. In 'fact, the truth of the matter is, that 95 to 96 per cent of contracts are reached through collective bargaining. A very small percentage end up in a strike or a lock-out. I remember when the longshoremen went out on the west coast. They appreciated then, as they do now, the difficulties that the grain producers of western Canada and the potash producers were having. So they went to the government, the Maritime Shippers Association and the port authorities and said: "Look, we will move grain. Our disagreement is not with the handling of bulk commodities. This strike is about containers, shift work and how far away we have to go to go to work". They said: "We'll move the grain". There would not have been a single bushel of grain left sitting.
You know what, Mr. Speaker? Management refused. Management refused to see the grain moving. Then I listened to the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek saying that we should have some kind of a law. Well, I can tell him the kind of law we should have. He mentioned marriage breakdowns and so on although I noticed he did not mention mortgage deals, like that happens as happened to the grain handlers and the employer says no, the law says the employer is going to have to do it anyway.
I am sad to say that even our own Prairie wheat pools would not agree to keep the grain moving even though the strike had nothing to do with the movement of grain. Why? Because the other shippers and owners were calling the shots.
Government Orders
I have something else I want to mention and I am glad the Minister of Veterans Affairs is still here, because I want to talk about what the cost of the strike is to the department, the government, Treasury Board or whoever. I have figures which I received from a reliable source. I would like him to check on it and tell us if it is true that the government is paying $50,000 a day for catering? Is it true that the government is paying $163,835 per week to provide extra security over and above what it is already paying for?
Can you imagine, $163,835 per week is what the government's stubbornness and the strike is costing. I would like to know if it is true or not. Nurses being hired from various agencies are costing $350,000 a week. That is what this strike is costing.
The government is currently paying in overtime at St. Anne de Bellevue $840,000 per week. The total cost to the employer during the strike is $1,633,835. Before the strike the cost was $385,000. In other words, the government is putting out $1,300,000 more than it was before. Even if the employees got all they were asking for these figures would only increase by 6 per cent whatever the cost would be of the human rights settlement.
Who do you think is getting that $163,835 for security? Pinkerton's, naturally, those friends of the working man for the last 150 years. Pinkerton's are getting an extra $163,835 a week. It pays to be friends of the government. This government has no objection. I want the minister to get up and tell us if these figures are inaccurate because we are looking at something over $2 million per week that he has frittered away because of his stubbornness and his refusal to be fair.
Some employees have not had an increase for three years. My goodness, it is a good thing he is not commanding a regiment under those kinds of terms because he would have to watch his back more than his front. The doctors are getting an extra $100 a day at St. Anne de Bellevue on weekends. Some of them are prepared to say, and we are looking for some of them, that the patients are starting to suffer. If that is true there is nobody else to blame but the Minister of Veterans Affairs. I can assure you we will find out.
The staff and nurses who are still working have been given an extra $300 each in overtime bonuses. I am assuming that those are bonuses over and above the overtime they made. The government has brought in 80

December 8, 1989
Government Orders
agency nurses at a total cost of wages, living expenses, travel et cetera of $500 per day each.
I think the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the President of the Treasury Board have something to answer for. How can they say that somehow or other this legislation is necessary because the unions are not being reasonable? The one not being reasonable is this government. The government is not being fair and is victimizing farmers and shippers as well as employees. It is this government and nobody else. You are the architects of your own problem and you are the perpetrators.
I have enjoyed doing this, although I did not relish it. I have enjoyed getting after these birds for what I have seen this government and the previous one do repeatedly. They never learn. Governments continue not to learn, and they will keep making the same mistakes.

Mr. Speaker, I have been listening to this debate all afternoon and I think there are some fundamental facts we are not putting forward. The government stated earlier today in one of the speeches settlement is equal to a 49 per cent increase over 36 months. The government talked about the fact that it cared for the quality of life in this country, about the fact that legislating these people back to work was for the greater public good. It talked about the fact that it cares about the deficit. It talked about the fact that the only reason we are here today is to oppose for the sake of opposing.
Well, I know we are here today to challenge this government's value system. To state that this is a 49 per cent increase over 3 years is really not putting the right face on this legislation. These men and women are making $18,000 a year and they have to be on standby 24 hours a day, seven days a week. They have to put their lives at stake because they are going to sea to rescue others. Obviously most of these rescue missions are at times when they are in danger. They must face twenty-five and thirty-foot waves.
People in my community in downtown Toronto cannot imagine that. These are waves two or three storeys high. We get three and four foot waves in Lake Ontario and we run the other way. These men and women who are at
sea are guarding our waters, our fisheries, and they are asking for 50 cents an hour more on a base of $18,000.
I cannot understand the logic of the government because I know there are many members on the other side who care. They are approachable, and they love this country as much as we do, but I think we are going to have to change our style in this House and when situations like this arise from time to time we are going to speak up. This has nothing to do with unions or government. These are basic values and we are just looking the other way.
I have never been on a coast guard vehicle. I probably would not have the guts to go on a coast guard vehicle on the high seas. However, I tried to imagine who in my community has a similar task, provides a similar public service that my constituents of Toronto can relate to. I thought of fire-fighters in Toronto, a group of men and women whom we are proud of and are on stand-by 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. They put their lives in danger for the public service. Their starting salary is $31,500. After five years on the job, a first-class fire-fighter receives $42,800.
We are here talking today about coast guard crew who are only making $18,000 a year. They are asking for approximately $2,000 a year more, 50 cents an hour. I cannot understand this, because when I think of a husband and a wife and maybe one or two children with the take-home pay of $18,000 to $20,000 a year which I calculate to be approximately $260 to $280 a week, I do not know how these men and women make a go of it.
We are sitting here in the national chamber, where we are supposed to have national standards, where the person in an outpost in Newfoundland has as much chance and as much opportunity and is given the same dignity as a person in downtown Toronto. This bill is not meeting that national test.
It is December, the Christmas season, and we are supposed to have a spirit of generosity. We are supposed to have a spirit of understanding. We are sitting here on a Friday afternoon arguing about 50 cents an hour for people who are putting their lives at stake.
I think, and I have seen this repeatedly with this government, that the government is really tearing away at the national will. It breaks down the national will by not showing respect for our human capital. In my mind
December 8, 1989

that is not only bad nation building but it is also bad economics. What of an incentive? What kind of motivation does one have? What kind of pride does one have in one's job when his employer does not think he is worth 50 cents an hour? I just cannot understand the logic.
The Prime Minister of Canada has a reputation for being one of the best deal makers in Canada. After an 11-hour marathon discussion with the premiers of Canada he was able to come through with a constitutional deal. Why can this same Prime Minister, who has children as I do and as do the fathers on coast guard crews who are risking their lives, not display the same leadership and ability to craft a deal? Why can he not do that on an issue like this one? It is a mystery to me. It escapes me.
That is another problem we have in this House. Sometimes we only pay attention to those voices, to those lobby groups and to those organizations that are well financed and the best organization behind their cause.
We are not in this chamber to oppose for the sake of opposing. We are here to oppose constructively. We are here to care about deficit and debt as is the government. Yes, we have made some mistakes in the past, but I must tell Your Honour that there is no excuse for us to be bantering back and forth today in this House for 50 cents an hour for men and women who go to high sea, without notice, saving lives of others, protecting our waterways and protecting our oceans. There is no excuse.
Sometimes the government becomes captive of officials who will tell it that we have to save 15 per cent of this budget and 10 per cent of that budget. They just calculate the gross amounts and they never see the human capital that exists behind those numbers. I believe this is another example where we are just looking at the gross numbers and we are not looking at the bottom line. The bottom line is the human capital, the men and women who put their lives at stake.
I do not want you to think that I am forgetting about hospital services. The hospital service system of this country is the envy of the world. If we are going to play around with the spirit, the attitude and the dignity of
Government Orders
hospital workers, I think we are putting a lot more at risk than the government realizes.
I want to repeat: we are not here to oppose for the sake of opposing. What we have today is a situation where there are people who are genuinely disadvantaged and it is our role to speak on their behalf. Again I repeat: a fireman in downtown Toronto after five years of service makes over $40,000 a year. The crews on the coast guard want $20,000.
We have got to be fair here. We have to be daring. The minister with the stroke of a pen could get an order out and deal with this situation immediately. We tend to forget because these organizations are not well organized as lobby groups, but we should prick our conscience and remind ourselves that we are here in this House not for the privileged but for the disadvantaged.
While I was listening to some of my colleagues speak today, I was going through one of my files and I was reminded of an old John Denver tune that I thought was rather appropriate. Even though I have never been on a coast guard ship and I have never met the men and women who have been on those ships or who have been to sea on rescue, it does not mean I cannot feel for them because I am from another region of this country.
I think John Denver says it best in his song It's About Time: "There is a man who is my brother, I just do not know his name, but I know his home and family, because I know we feel the same. And it hurts me when he is hungry and when his children cry for I too am a father; that little one is mine. It is about time we begin to turn the world around. It is about time we realized this is the family of man. It is about time, it is about changes".

speakerposition: Liberal Party Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that we will all have an opportunity again next week to discuss this, because of the unprecedented decision taken by the opposition members to ensure that this bill not only will not receive the support of both the liberal party and the other opposition party in the House of Commons, but will not receive any assistance facilitating the bill. We will all have an opportunity again next week to deal with this matter.

December 8, 1989
Government Orders
I simply want to point out very briefly on behalf of opposition members that the long-standing tradition of this place when this kind of legislation is brought before Parliament is that very often, opposition parties vote against it. But very seldom, in fact I cannot think of a precedent, do opposition parties actually behave in a manner that forces the government into using closure on back to work legislation.
I hope Canadians will reflect on this and realize that this decision is a direct result of the contemplation, of the searching of one's conscience, individually and collectively, and of the conclusion that the government has not bargained fairly with public servants in critical sectors, both ships crews and hospital services workers who are, comparatively speaking, among the lowest paid, given the value of their work, employees in Canada. They have asked for nothing but a fair break.
In the case of ships' crews, they have responded in every instance they could with the emergency search and rescue services, and have conducted search and rescue. They have saved lives by laying down their pickets during the course of the strike.
In the case of hospital services workers, they have offered to provide emergency service and have been rebutted, refused, by the employer.
Canadians who are wondering what is going on this afternoon should realize that process is unprecedented in Canadian parliamentary history. It is a profound statement by members of Parliament who sit in opposition benches-and it is an extremely unusual statement-that there comes a time when the power of government, the big hammer of government, should not be wielded against ordinary citizens, against employees of the people of Canada, not employees of government, not employees of the party in power, but employees of the people of Canada.
There comes a time to stand up, notwithstanding the tremendous political power represented opposite by a majority government, notwithstanding the tremendous pressure coming from corporate Canada, for those who are least able to defend themselves, particularly when they have bargained in good faith and they have been faced with a government that has but one plan and that is to destroy fundamentally their right to collective bargaining.
It is for that reason that we in this party, the Liberal Party of Canada, refused unanimous consent to allow the
introduction of this bill, this draconian measure, by the minister responsible for the Treasury Board. We stood up, the Liberal Party of Canada, and we said no, there shall be no unanimous consent.
We say to the government that it is Friday and the weekend is upon us. We want a quick settlement to this strike. We do not want ships tied up in the St. Lawrence. We do not want patients at hospitals having anything less than the full services they should have. We do not want the potential of health and safety being put at risk. We do not want commerce to stop. We do not want trade to be affected.
We want Canada to function smoothly, but we are not willing to sell out the ordinary employees to the power of a government which wants to paint as villains those employees who are hard-working, selfless individuals asking for a fair shake. We are not willing to sell them out as villains to a government that behaves in a villainous manner.
We say to the government, if you want, as we want, a quick settlement, then go to the table with justice in your heart. Go to the table with a commitment to a fair deal, not necessarily a gracious deal but just a fair deal. If you want a quick settlement to the strike, resolve it at the bargaining table because that is where this issue belongs, not with back to work legislation.
We say to the government at the end of a day, a Friday, we will be back here again Monday. There will be no quick passage. We are going to fight for these employees. If you want a settlement that is right and just, sit man to man, woman to woman, across the table and settle it like human beings. Put away the hammer.
Hear, hear!
